---
title: "After PHP Gate: A Blueprint for the Static Web"
url: https://raskell.io/articles/a-blueprint-for-the-static-web/
author: Raffael Schneider
date: 2026-10-26
description: "Last week's PHP flaws reached every PHP installation serving web requests. My blueprint for sites and apps that run no code per request at all."
tags: [applied-security, edge-systems, open-web, zola, webassembly, rust, context-engineering]
---

# After PHP Gate: A Blueprint for the Static Web

## In short

PHP Gate, two critical remote code execution flaws in every PHP installation serving web requests, showed the risk of running code on a server for each request to produce a page that is almost always the same. My blueprint is to render at commit time, serve files from the edge, and run code only where it cannot be avoided: in the visitor's browser or in a small edge function that does one job. Across about forty of my own projects I found the same eleven practices, from writing the agent context and declaring the ontology first to pinned tools, machine-legible pages and a strict Content Security Policy. Some projects genuinely need a backend, such as those with accounts, many writers or real-time collaboration, and then I pick Go, Next.js, Phoenix or Refrakt by the shape of the problem while keeping the rest static. The safest runtime is the one you never start; two template repositories, *blueprint-site* and *blueprint-app*, put the practices into files, and I admit my own sites do not all follow them yet.

Last Wednesday, the PHP project shipped [four releases in one afternoon](https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php).
PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 fixed two flaws that allow unauthenticated remote code execution, both rated
critical at CVSS 9.2:

- [CVE-2026-109618](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-109618), "RCE via OOM corruption"
  ([GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w](https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w))
- [CVE-2026-109619](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-109619), "RCE via stale global state"
  ([GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp](https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp))

[The advisory](https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php) is short and does not leave much room for interpretation: the
flaws affect "all PHP installations serving web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP
and LiteSpeed," and "there are no complete mitigations, updating is the only safe choice." Details had
[leaked a day before the embargo lifted](https://threatlandscape.io/blog/php-core-rce-cve-2026-109618-109619-leak-ahead-of-embargo),
honeypots started seeing attempts soon after, and for the rest of the week hosting providers, agencies and WordPress
admins were patching, checking, and patching again. Most people call the flaws
[PHP2Shell](https://threatlandscape.io/blog/php-core-rce-cve-2026-109618-109619-leak-ahead-of-embargo). I have been
calling the week PHP Gate.

The scale is what makes it a gate rather than a bug. PHP runs
[69.2% of the websites](https://w3techs.com/technologies/details/pl-php) whose server-side language W3Techs can
identify, and WordPress alone runs [39.6% of all websites](https://w3techs.com/technologies/details/cm-wordpress). Laravel, MediaWiki (so, Wikipedia), Drupal, Magento: the
productive web is still, to a large degree, a PHP interpreter that executes for every single request. When the
interpreter has a hole, every one of those requests is a way in.

I do not want to pile on PHP. The PHP team handled this well, and the language has carried more of the web than any
other. What worries me is a habit that goes far beyond PHP: running code on a server, at request time, to produce a
page that is almost always the same page it produced a second ago. Most of the sites caught up in PHP Gate could
have been a folder of files, with no runtime for anyone to attack.

This post is the blueprint I use instead. I looked at every web project I have built over the last few years, about
forty sites, documentation sites and web apps across several GitHub organisations, and wrote down what they all do.
The practices turned out to be the same every time. There are two template repositories at the end you can clone.
The blueprint is not the answer to everything, either, so there is also a section on when a project needs a real
backend, and what I build those with.

If "static" and "dynamic" are fuzzy terms for you, read the next section first; it explains them without assuming
anything. If you build websites for a living, skip ahead to [the shape of it](#the-shape-of-it).

## Static and dynamic, in plain words

Every time you open a web page, your browser asks a computer somewhere (a **server**) for it, and the server sends
back a file of HTML that the browser draws. The difference between a static and a dynamic website is *when that file
is made*.

A **dynamic** website makes the page at the moment you ask for it. A program on the server (WordPress, written in PHP,
is the most common one) reads a template, asks a database for the article, fills the article into the template, and
sends you the result. Then it does the same thing again for the next visitor, and the next, usually producing exactly
the same page. It is a kitchen that cooks every plate to order, even when everybody orders the same dish.

```
dynamic:  you ──► server ──► PHP runs ──► database ──► page is assembled ──► you
                  (for every visitor, every time)
```

A **static** website makes every page once, ahead of time, whenever the content changes. A program called a **static
site generator** (this site uses one called Zola) reads all the articles and templates and writes out a folder of
finished HTML files. That folder is copied to a **CDN**, a network of servers around the world that does nothing but
hand out files quickly from somewhere close to you. When you ask for a page, nothing is cooked. The finished file is
simply handed over.

```
static:   writer ──► build, once per change ──► folder of files ──► CDN
          you ──► CDN ──► the finished file ──► you
                  (nothing runs when you visit)
```

Static does not mean boring or frozen. A static page can still be interactive, because the interactivity runs in
*your* browser: menus, search, maps, even a chess engine. What a static site does not have is a program on a server
that runs because you visited, which is the part PHP Gate attacked.

A few more words this post uses, so they do not get in the way later:

- **Edge** means the CDN's servers close to the reader. An **edge function** (Cloudflare calls them **Workers**) is a
  small program that runs there, for the rare jobs a file cannot do, like accepting a form.
- **Build** is the step that turns content and templates into the finished files. It runs when a change is merged, not
  when someone visits.
- **Backend** is a program on a server that the website talks to: it stores data, checks passwords, takes payments.
  A static site has no backend of its own; an app may still need one.
- **WebAssembly** lets code written in languages like Rust run inside the browser, close to the speed of a native
  program.
- **Agents** are AI assistants that read websites on someone's behalf. They read static pages especially well.

## The idea in one paragraph

Render at commit time, serve files from the edge, and run code only where it cannot be avoided. A page is built once,
when a change is merged, and from then on it is a file on a CDN. Logic that must react to a visitor moves to one of
two places: the visitor's own browser (JavaScript, or Rust compiled to WebAssembly when the work is heavy), or a small
edge function that does exactly one job, the pattern I described in
[Edge Systems Are the New Backend](https://raskell.io/articles/edge-systems-are-the-new-backend/). There is no application server, no database behind the pages, and no
runtime to patch at two in the morning, because there is nothing running between the request and the file.

## Why bother

**Security.** A static page cannot be exploited the way PHP Gate was exploited, because a request for it never
executes anything. The attack surface shrinks to the CDN (which is someone else's full-time job), the build (which
runs in a throwaway container on merge, not on request), and whatever edge functions you choose to add. On most of my
sites that last list has zero or one entries. You still have a supply chain to care about, which is why pinning and
review matter so much later in this post, but you no longer have an interpreter facing the internet.

**Operations.** A static site has no server of its own to patch, scale or restart. During PHP Gate my static sites
needed nothing from me. A traffic spike is the CDN's problem, and the CDN was built for it. Rollback is a redeploy of
the previous commit, a single click in the Pages dashboard.

**Speed and cost.** Files from an edge cache are as fast as the web gets, and serving them costs next to nothing:
Cloudflare Pages hosts a static site on its free plan with up to 20,000 files.

**Longevity.** A folder of HTML ages better than almost any other software. Sites I built years ago still render
exactly as they did, with no framework upgrade, no runtime end of life, no database migration. PHP 8.2 reaches end of
life on 31 December; a static site has no such date.

**Machines.** More of my readers are now agents, and static pages are simple for them to fetch and parse. If you
also publish each page as Markdown and describe it with structured data, they read it correctly.

There are real counterarguments:

- **Dynamic features.** Comments, forms, search, accounts, payments. Most of them have a static-friendly form:
  search runs in the browser over a prebuilt index, forms post to an edge function, comments become pull requests or
  issues. Some things genuinely need a server, and then you should run one; the [next section](#when-you-do-need-a-backend)
  is about those. The point is to run it for those things only, not for every page view.
- **Editors who do not use Git.** This is the real reason WordPress wins in many organisations, and the blueprint does
  not fully solve it. GitHub's web editor and issue forms get non-technical contributors surprisingly far, and an
  agent can turn a Word document into a pull request. For a newsroom with forty editors, I would think harder.
- **Vendor dependence.** I lean on Cloudflare. Everything I deploy is still just files in Git, so moving hosts is an
  afternoon. This site is served by GitHub Pages behind Cloudflare, and every push goes to Codeberg as well as
  GitHub.
- **Build times.** A large site takes minutes to build, not milliseconds to render. My largest project takes about a
  minute for ten languages; Cloudflare's build limit is twenty minutes. Precomputing data in separate build steps
  keeps it there.

## When you do need a backend

Some projects are not websites with a few interactive parts. They are services, and pretending otherwise produces a
pile of edge functions that slowly turns into a backend nobody designed. These are the signs I look for:

- **People have accounts and their own data.** Logins, profiles, private documents, per-user settings that must follow
  them across devices.
- **Many people write, not just read.** A marketplace, a forum, a booking system, an internal tool where every user
  changes shared state.
- **Things happen in real time between users.** Chat, collaborative editing, live dashboards, presence.
- **The work is heavy, long, or secret.** Jobs that run for minutes, data that cannot be shipped to the browser,
  integrations that need credentials, money moving between parties.
- **The data does not fit in a build.** Millions of records that change by the minute cannot be rendered into files
  on every merge.

When two or more of these are true, I build a backend, and I pick it by the shape of the problem:

| The project | What I reach for | Why |
|---|---|---|
| An API: endpoints, data, integrations | **Go** | One static binary, a fast start, modest memory, an excellent standard library for HTTP, and concurrency that is easy to reason about. |
| A rich app frontend that renders per user | **Next.js**, or a framework like it | Server rendering where a page depends on who is looking, static export where it does not, and the largest ecosystem of components and people. |
| A service that is distributed by nature: real time, many connections, many nodes | **Elixir and Phoenix** | The BEAM was built for exactly this: lightweight processes, supervision that restarts what fails, clustering, PubSub and LiveView without bolting on extra infrastructure. |
| The same, with a type system that catches mistakes at compile time | **[Refrakt](https://refrakt.raskell.io)** | My own framework, in Gleam on the BEAM: productive like Phoenix, explicit like Gleam, with generators for the routine parts. Still young; I use it where I can follow its changes. |

Two of my own services show the Phoenix row in practice: [Cyanea](https://cyanea.bio) runs Phoenix on SQLite, and
[Archipelag.io](https://archipelag.io) runs Phoenix with Postgres and NATS. Both run on one bare-metal server, which I
wrote about in [How AI Makes Bare Metal Viable Again](https://raskell.io/articles/how-ai-makes-bare-metal-viable-again/).

Even with a backend, most of the blueprint still applies. A service with a real backend has parts that are just
content: the landing page, the documentation, the changelog, the legal pages, the blog. Those stay static, on the
blueprint, and the backend is a separate deployment with a small, well-defined API. The rest of the lessons carry over
unchanged: agent context first, the data types declared before the code, pinned versions, and as little running at
request time as the problem allows. And keep the PHP Gate lesson close: a backend is a runtime facing the internet,
so it needs an owner, an update routine, and the discipline to keep it no bigger than it has to be.

## The shape of it

Every project of mine, from a one-page product site to a ten-language knowledge base, has the same shape:

```
  GitHub organisation (one per product)
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ .github   .claude  theme  content   site    app     worker │
  │ profile   context  Zola   Markdown  config  Svelte  edge   │
  │ policies  rules    Tera   + data    build   + Rust  logic  │
  └───────────────────┬──────┬─────────┬───────┬───────┬───────┘
                      └──────┴─────────┤       │       │
                                       │       │       │    theme and content: submodules,
                                       ▼       ▼       ▼           pinned and reviewed
                                 ┌───────────────────┐┌─────────┐
                                 │ Cloudflare Pages  ││ Workers │
                                 │ files at the edge ││ one job │
                                 └─────────┬─────────┘└────┬────┘
                                           ▼               ▼
                    readers and agents: HTML, Markdown, JSON-LD, llms.txt
```

Content, presentation and distribution live apart. The content repository holds Markdown and data and nothing else.
The theme repository holds templates and styles. The site repository pins both as git submodules, adds
configuration, and is the thing Cloudflare builds. Apps get their own repository, and edge functions either live next
to the site or in their own. Each repository has one job, so each one is small enough to reason about, and an agent
working in it does not have to load the world.

## The practices

I found eleven practices that every mature project of mine follows, and that the younger ones are converging on.
They are listed roughly in the order I set them up.

### 1. Start with the agent context, before the first line of code

The first file in every repository is `AGENTS.md`, and in a Claude Code project `CLAUDE.md` simply imports it
(`@AGENTS.md`) and adds the Claude-specific parts. I write it before any code, as the contract the repository works
under: the stack, where each kind of content is registered, what is generated and must never be
edited, how to verify a change, and the rules that always hold. On this site it starts like this:

```markdown
The short version: **content is registered once, in a source file; everything else is generated.**
Never edit a generated file by hand. If a new piece of content does not show up somewhere it should,
the fix is in the source file or in the generator, not in the output.
```

Then come the rules, in `.claude/rules/`, one file per kind of task (content, templates, Rust), each scoped to the
paths it applies to. Then skills, in `.claude/skills/`, for the workflows that repeat: add a page end to end, publish
an article, translate. My most mature project goes further: an organisation-level context repository that every
repository's `AGENTS.md` points to, subagents with restricted tools (the reviewer is read-only and forms its verdict
before it sees the editor's report), and an explicit list of changes that require a human.

Writing it first costs an hour. In return, every later session, mine or an agent's, starts from the same
understanding, and the decisions the rest of this list depends on are made before they are needed.

### 2. Declare the ontology before you write the content

Every site knows a small number of kinds of thing: articles, notes, projects, talks, books, topics. I declare them up
front, each with its register (where instances live), its required fields, its allowed values, and the schema.org
type it becomes for machines. In the blueprint this is `data/kinds.toml`:

```toml
[kinds.article]
register = "content/articles/"
required = ["title", "date", "description", "taxonomies.topics"]
optional = ["updated", "draft", "extra.author", "extra.image"]
jsonld = "BlogPosting"

[kinds.project]
register = "data/projects.toml"
required = ["slug", "title", "description", "status", "url", "topics"]
jsonld = "SoftwareApplication"
enum.status = ["live", "beta", "early", "archived"]
```

A validator enforces it on every pull request, using only the Python standard library so it runs anywhere. Unknown
fields fail, so a typo in `descripton` cannot silently drop a page's description. Topics come from one vocabulary,
with `broader` links that turn the vocabulary into a small graph. On this site the same declarations drive the
[map](https://raskell.io/map/) (the story of how it came about is in [This Site Is Becoming a Map](https://raskell.io/articles/this-site-is-becoming-a-map/)),
the search index, the JSON-LD and the [ontology page](https://raskell.io/ontology/) that explains all of it to readers.

The payoff is that nothing is improvised later. When I add a reading log, a talk, or a new kind of project, the
question is "what kind is it, and where is it registered," not "where should I put this file."

### 3. One GitHub organisation per product, one job per repository

A personal account mixes everything. An organisation gives a product its own members, its own secrets, its own
profile, and room for the repositories it will grow into. I start with the same set:

| Repository | Job |
|---|---|
| `.github` | Organisation profile, shared issue forms, `SECURITY.md`, contributing guide |
| `.claude` | Organisation-wide agent context: rules, skills, decisions, plans |
| `theme` | The Zola theme, versioned on its own |
| `content` | Markdown and data, validated in CI |
| `site` | Configuration and build, pins theme and content as submodules |
| `app`, `worker` | Only when the product needs them |

Two rules keep this healthy. Submodule URLs are HTTPS, so the Cloudflare build can clone them without SSH keys. And
the theme is never copied into a site: I found one organisation where five copies of a theme had drifted from the
original in fourteen to eighteen template files each. A submodule pin makes drift a visible commit instead of an
invisible fork.

### 4. GitHub is the content store and the moderation layer

There is no admin panel, because Git already is one. Every change is a pull request with a diff, a review and a
history. `CODEOWNERS` says who must approve changes to content, headers and edge code. An issue form collects
corrections with a required URL and a dropdown for what is wrong. Contributors submit a pull request from a fork, and
the validator runs before a human looks.

Reader input lands in the same place. The blueprint's only edge function takes the feedback form from every page and
files it as a GitHub issue in the content repository, with mentions defused so nobody can ping your team through your
own site. Feedback, corrections and contributions all end up in one queue, moderated by the same people with the same
tools, and nothing a stranger types ever reaches a page without a review.

Put together, every change follows the same path, whoever starts it:

```
  reader      ──► feedback form ──► Worker ──► GitHub issue ──► triaged ──┐
  editor      ──► branch ─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  contributor ──► fork ───────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
                                                                          │
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ▼
  pull request to the content repository
  │   CI validates the ontology, builds the site, runs the tests
  ▼
  review and approval by CODEOWNERS, then merge to main
  │   a workflow in the content repository calls the Pages deploy hook
  ▼
  Pages rebuilds the site ──► new files on the CDN
```

When content lives in its own repository, one small workflow in it closes the loop: on every push to `main`, it calls
the Pages deploy hook, and the site rebuilds with the new content. Without it, a merged correction waits for the
next unrelated site change.

### 5. Zola, pinned, through mise

Zola is a single binary with no plugin ecosystem to keep patched, it builds this site in a few seconds, and its Tera
templates are expressive enough for everything on this list: the map, the JSON-LD, the topic pages, the Markdown
copies. The one thing to get right is the version. My survey found Zola 0.19, 0.19.2, 0.21, 0.22.1 and 0.23.6 across
my own sites, and the newest release changed its template engine enough that my templates no longer build on it. So
the version is pinned in `mise.toml`, and CI and the Cloudflare build read the same pin:

```toml
[tools]
# 0.23 replaced the template engine; these templates target 0.22.
# Upgrade on purpose, in its own change, never because a machine has a newer zola on PATH.
zola = "0.22.1"
python = "3.13.17"

[tasks.build]
depends = ["check", "llms", "security-txt"]
run = "zola build"
```

mise doubles as the task runner, so `mise run check`, `mise run build` and `mise run dev` mean the same thing on my
laptop, in CI, on Cloudflare and for an agent.

### 6. Cloudflare Pages, and know its limits before it tells you

Pages connects to the GitHub repository, builds on every push, and gives every pull request a preview URL. The build
command is a short script that installs the pinned tools and runs `mise run build`. Two files in `static/` do the
rest: `_headers` for security and caching, `_redirects` to keep old URLs alive when content moves.

The limits are generous and still worth checking locally, because the failure is quiet: 25 MiB per file, 20,000 files
per site on the free plan (100,000 on paid plans), 100 header rules, a twenty-minute build. My most mature project
keeps an incident log of every time one of these bit, each entry with the local check that would have caught it. The
blueprint's build script ends with two of those checks, so an oversized WebAssembly file or a file explosion fails in
CI instead of at upload:

```sh
big=$(find public -type f -size +25M | head -1); [ -z "$big" ] || { echo "too large for Pages: $big"; exit 1; }
n=$(find public -type f | wc -l); [ "$n" -lt 20000 ] || { echo "too many files for Pages: $n"; exit 1; }
```

### 7. Workers only for what a file cannot do

An edge function is the right tool when something needs state, a secret, or a protocol. My Workers each do one thing:
accept a form, proxy two country domains onto language prefixes, sync [Kurumi](https://kurumi.raskell.io), an offline
notes app, to object storage, run [Arcanist](https://arcanist.sh)'s package registry, or serve an MCP server over a
static JSON API. They are small, read-only where
they can be, cached, and hold at most one narrowly scoped secret (`wrangler secret put`, never the repository).

The feedback Worker in the blueprint is about sixty lines and does the job a contact form plugin used to do: it checks
the origin, rate-limits per address, drops bots that fill a hidden field, validates the message, and opens one issue
with a fine-grained token that can do nothing else. Its tests run with `node --test` against a stubbed GitHub, so the
logic is checked without deploying anything.

### 8. Apps are static too: Svelte, prerendered, with a service worker

When a project is an app rather than a site, I still ship files. SvelteKit with the static adapter prerenders every
route, and the result deploys to Pages exactly like a Zola site. Svelte compiles away most of its runtime, which
keeps the bundle small, and its runes keep local state in plain variables.

Offline support is what makes an app usable on a train or a plane. SvelteKit's own service worker is enough,
without a plugin. The pattern I use everywhere: one cache per deploy, named after the build version so a new
deploy never mixes with an old one; hashed assets cache-first, because their content can never change; pages
network-first with the cache as the fallback. My language-learning app, [Manabi](https://manabi.raskell.io), goes further and picks a strategy per kind of
data, stale-while-revalidate for dictionary shards and network-only for the user's own API calls. Only three of my
apps had a service worker at all. All of them should.

### 9. Rust compiled to WebAssembly, for the right reasons

When an app needs real computation, a chess engine, a neural simulation like [Hotaru](https://hotaru.raskell.io), a
config validator, I write it in Rust and compile it to WebAssembly. The layout is always the same: a core crate with no wasm or JavaScript in it, tested with
plain `cargo test`, and a thin crate that exports a C ABI over it. No wasm-bindgen unless a framework needs it. The
browser reads results straight out of the module's linear memory. A release profile with fat LTO, one codegen unit
and `panic = "abort"`, then `wasm-opt`, keeps modules small: the blueprint's is 16 KB, and the build fails if it grows
past its budget. Heavy work runs in a Web Worker, so the page never freezes.

```
  main thread               Web Worker                     WebAssembly module
  ┌──────────────┐          ┌──────────────────┐           ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ Svelte UI    │ message  │ render.worker.js │ C ABI     │ crates/wasm          │
  │              ├─────────►│                  ├──────────►│   numbers in, a      │
  │ never blocks │          │ calls in bands   │           │   pointer out        │
  │              │◄─────────┤ of rows          │◄──────────┤                      │
  └──────────────┘ pixels,  └──────────────────┘ reads     │ crates/core          │
                   transferred                   linear    │   plain Rust,        │
                   not copied                    memory    │   tested natively    │
                                                           └──────────────────────┘
```

I wanted the blueprint to show the speed-up, so I measured it. It renders the same Mandelbrot image in Rust and in
JavaScript, side by side, and on that tight floating-point loop Chrome's JavaScript engine was as fast as
WebAssembly: 73 ms against 75 to 92 ms. The first WebAssembly run even took 192 ms, because V8 starts WebAssembly in a
baseline compiler and cannot move a running call onto optimised code, so one long call never gets fast. Rendering in
bands of rows, many short calls instead of one long one, brought it to parity.

The reasons to use Rust in the browser lie elsewhere:

- **One core, many places.** [Zentinel](https://zentinelproxy.io)'s documentation validates every configuration
  snippet in the browser with the real configuration parser (the proxy itself is the subject of
  [What Zentinel Is Really Optimizing For](https://raskell.io/articles/what-zentinel-is-really-optimizing-for/)), compiled to WebAssembly from the same crate the proxy
  uses. A snippet that would not load in production shows red on the page. The same Rust that runs in a server or a
  desktop app runs in the tab, tested once.
- **Types at the boundary.** The only interface between JavaScript and the logic is a handful of typed numbers and a
  pointer. Everything behind it is checked by the compiler.
- **The work JavaScript is bad at.** 64-bit integer arithmetic, bit boards, tight memory layouts, threads.
  [Kishi](https://kishi.raskell.io)'s chess engine is that kind of code; [Learning to Play](https://raskell.io/articles/learning-to-play/)
  is the long story of building it.

### 10. Make it legible to machines

Agents read the web for people now, and a static site is simple for them to read. Every site of mine ships the same
kit:

- `llms.txt` at the root, an index of the site in Markdown, and `llms-full.txt` with the full text.
- A Markdown copy of every page at its URL with `.md`, linked from the page with
  `<link rel="alternate" type="text/markdown">`, served with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`.
- JSON-LD on every page, typed by the ontology: BlogPosting, SoftwareApplication, DefinedTerm, Review, Dataset.
- `robots.txt` with a single group and a Content-Signal line that says what the content may be used for.
- `.well-known/`: `security.txt` with an expiry that a build step keeps a year ahead, an RFC 9727 API catalog, and an
  `auth.md` that states nothing needs authentication, so an agent treats a 403 as a fault, not a policy.
- Where it pays off: a WebMCP script that registers in-browser tools only when an agent is present, an MCP server
  over the static JSON API, IndexNow pings after deploy.

None of this is heavy. It is a few templates and one script that runs before the build, and it means an agent quoting
your site quotes the page, not a scrape of it.

The same discipline covers people who use assistive technology: one `h1`, a skip link, visible focus, labels on
icon-only buttons and canvases, motion only under `prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference`, and every page working
without JavaScript, with scripts adding to it rather than building it.

### 11. Security is mostly saying no

A static site gets most of its security from what it does not do, and the rest from a few lines of configuration:

- **A strict Content Security Policy.** `default-src 'none'`, scripts and styles from `'self'` only, no
  `unsafe-inline`, no `unsafe-eval`. On a Zola site that is easy: no inline scripts, structured data is a JSON block
  the policy does not touch. On a SvelteKit app, `csp.mode = "hash"` hashes the framework's one inline script, and the
  single inline style its screen-reader announcer needs is allowed by its hash with `'unsafe-hashes'`. WebAssembly
  needs `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` and nothing broader.
- **No third parties.** Self-hosted fonts or the system stack, no CDN scripts, no analytics on the page.
- **No secrets in the client.** If a feature needs a key, it is a Worker with one scoped secret, or the user brings
  their own key and it never leaves their browser.
- **Pinned everything.** Tools in `mise.toml`, the Rust toolchain in `rust-toolchain.toml`, npm packages to exact
  versions, GitHub Actions to commit SHAs, with Dependabot proposing the updates as pull requests.
- **Review as a control.** Nothing reaches `main` without a pull request, and the people in `CODEOWNERS` approve
  changes to headers and edge code.

## Hands-on: the blueprint in an afternoon

The two template repositories put all of the above into files:
[blueprint-site](https://github.com/raskell-io/blueprint-site) (Zola, the ontology, the agent context, the machine
kit, the feedback Worker) and [blueprint-app](https://github.com/raskell-io/blueprint-app) (SvelteKit, the service
worker, the Rust core and its WebAssembly boundary). Both build on a fresh clone. These are the steps, in order.

**1. Create the organisation and its first repositories.** On GitHub, create an organisation for the product, then:

```sh
gh repo create your-org/.github --public
gh repo create your-org/site --public --template raskell-io/blueprint-site --clone
cd site
```

**2. Give it context first.** Edit `AGENTS.md`: the product in one sentence, the stack table, the registers. Keep
`CLAUDE.md` as `@AGENTS.md` plus what is specific to Claude. Delete the rules you do not need, add the ones you do.

**3. Declare the ontology.** Edit `data/kinds.toml` until it lists every kind your site will have, and
`data/topics.toml` until it holds your vocabulary. Then run the validator:

```sh
mise install
mise run check
# check_content: ontology holds
```

Then break something on purpose, to see what a mistake looks like. A note with a misspelled field, an undefined
topic and a file name with capitals gets this:

```
content/notes/Bad_Note.md: file name must be a lowercase slug with hyphens
content/notes/Bad_Note.md: missing required field `description` for a note
content/notes/Bad_Note.md: unknown field `descripton` (a note has date, description, draft, taxonomies.topics, title, updated)
content/notes/Bad_Note.md: topic `php` is not defined in data/topics.toml
check_content: 4 problem(s)
```

**4. Write, build, look.**

```sh
mise run dev      # http://127.0.0.1:1111, with drafts
mise run build    # public/: pages, feed, sitemap, llms.txt, .md copies, security.txt
```

Open a page, view its source, and find its JSON-LD; open `/llms.txt`; open the page's URL with `.md` at the end.

**5. Split the theme and the content into their own repositories** once the site works:

```sh
gh repo create your-org/theme --public && gh repo create your-org/content --public
git subtree split --prefix=themes/blueprint -b theme && git push git@github.com:your-org/theme.git theme:main
git subtree split --prefix=content -b content && git push git@github.com:your-org/content.git content:main
git rm -r themes/blueprint content && git commit -m "Theme and content move to their own repositories"
git submodule add https://github.com/your-org/theme.git themes/blueprint
git submodule add https://github.com/your-org/content.git content
```

**6. Connect Cloudflare Pages.** Workers & Pages, Create, Pages, Connect to Git, pick `your-org/site`. Build command
`bash scripts/cf-pages-build.sh`, output directory `public`. Add the custom domain in the project. Create a deploy
hook under Settings, Builds, and store it as `CF_PAGES_DEPLOY_HOOK` in the content repository, with the
`rebuild-site` workflow from the blueprint.

**7. Deploy the Worker,** if you want reader feedback:

```sh
cd worker
npx wrangler secret put GITHUB_TOKEN   # fine-grained: Issues read and write, on the content repo only
npx wrangler deploy
```

**8. Check the headers in production,** because a header that did not apply fails silently:

```sh
curl -sI https://your-domain/ | grep -iE "content-security-policy|x-content-type|referrer|link"
```

For an app, start from `blueprint-app` instead: `mise run test` runs the Rust core's tests and clippy, `mise run
build` builds the WebAssembly module within its budget and then the static app, and the same Pages setup deploys it.

## What I still get wrong

Writing this meant auditing my own projects, and they do not all follow the list. Most of my product sites have no
Content Security Policy, and the few that do still allow inline scripts. Several load fonts from Google, which
contradicts my own theme's "no external requests." Zola versions drift across five releases. Some product sites have
no CI at all and rely on Cloudflare's build to notice problems. Content pushes in my largest project do not trigger a
rebuild, and its CSP still carries `unsafe-inline`. The blueprints are the version where each of those is fixed, and I
am moving the rest of my projects onto them one by one.

## The takeaway

PHP Gate was a week of emergency patching for a large part of the web, and for most of the affected sites, nothing
about their content needed a server in the first place. The safest runtime is the one you never start. Build your
pages when you merge, serve them as files, and keep code for the places it actually has to run. When a project truly
needs a server, give it a real backend, built for the job, and keep everything around it static.

# Learning to Play

## In short

Reading *The Infinity Machine*, I was struck that the three parts in the chess handbook a young Demis Hassabis read are still the whole of a chess program, except that evaluation is now learned. Chess, shogi and Go trace the history of game AI: the classical method works in chess, strains in shogi where the NNUE network was invented, and fails in Go without networks guiding search. I built engines for all three in Rust, compiled to WebAssembly so they play offline on my phone, because a network inside the search has to be small, hand-written arithmetic. My self-play network beat the hand-written chess evaluation at equal search depth but only drew at equal time, because it costs more per position. The month left me with better questions than I started with, and I am keeping a notebook of every run, failures included, that may become a series.

This month I have been reading [*The Infinity Machine*](https://raskell.io/reading/#the-infinity-machine), Sebastian Mallaby's biography of Demis Hassabis, the chess prodigy from North London who founded DeepMind, the laboratory behind AlphaGo and AlphaFold. I picked it up because I wanted to understand one of the early architects of the AI we now live with, told by someone who had thirty hours of his time, and because almost everything that interests me, games, simulations, the question of what a machine can learn on its own, runs through his story. A hundred pages in, there is a scene I have not been able to put down.

It is 1988 and Hassabis is twelve. He has bought a Commodore Amiga 500 with his chess winnings, and in Foyles, the big bookshop on Charing Cross Road, he finds a slim paperback: *The Chess Computer Handbook* by David Levy. He reads it in one sitting. Levy explains how a chess program is built from three parts. The board has to be turned into numbers. A function has to look at a position and say who is better. And a search has to try moves, and the replies to them, and the replies to those, cutting off the branches that are obviously bad because the tree grows faster than any computer can follow. Hassabis tries to build it, finds that the Amiga chokes on chess, and writes an Othello program instead, which beats his five-year-old brother.

I put the book down at that point, partly because I recognised the boy a little, and partly because I realised two things. The first is that those three parts are still the whole of a chess program. Thirty-eight years later, the strongest engines in the world are a board in numbers, an evaluation function, and a tree search with pruning; what has changed is that the evaluation function is now learned by a machine rather than written by a person, and that the machine learned it by playing against itself. The second is that the laptop on my desk has thirty thousand times the memory of that Amiga, and I had never built the three parts myself.

So I did, this month. I wrote three game engines in Rust, for chess, for Japanese shogi, and for Go, compiled them to WebAssembly so they play in a browser on my phone, and built the training loop that is supposed to make one of them stronger than I could make it by hand. The app is at [kishi.raskell.io](https://kishi.raskell.io) and the code is [on GitHub](https://github.com/raskell-io/kishi). This is an account of why those three games, why those tools, and what happened when the ideas in the books met one ordinary machine.

## The book, the man and the lab

Mallaby is not a technology writer by trade. He is a former contributing editor of the *Financial Times*, twice a Pulitzer finalist, now a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, and his earlier books were about money: hedge funds in *More Money Than God*, Alan Greenspan in *The Man Who Knew*, venture capital in *The Power Law*. That turns out to be the right background. *The Infinity Machine* is a biography and a company history at once, built on about thirty hours of conversation with Hassabis and more than a hundred interviews around him, and it takes the question of why someone would build a technology they believe to be dangerous as seriously as the question of how. It came out earlier this year. I am reading it slowly, and the AlphaGo chapters are still ahead of me, which I find I do not mind, because I would rather meet them with my own version of the thing running.

Hassabis, if you do not follow the field, is the person it now treats as its elder statesman, at fifty. Born in Finchley in 1976 to a Singaporean Chinese mother and a Greek Cypriot father, he was a chess master at thirteen and the second-strongest player of his age in the world. At sixteen he was co-writing *Theme Park* at the games studio Bullfrog, a game that sold millions. He read computer science at Cambridge, ran a games studio of his own for seven years, and then went back to university for a doctorate in neuroscience, because he thought the only way to build an intelligent machine was to understand the one existing example first. In 2010, in an attic on Russell Square, he founded DeepMind with Shane Legg and Mustafa Suleyman, at a time when almost nobody in the field believed that what they proposed was possible. The first real money came from a Peter Thiel fund whose partners rated the science A-plus and the business model an F.

DeepMind was conceived as a Manhattan Project for artificial intelligence, and its method is what connects the book to this article. The bet was to combine two branches of the field that were both unfashionable in 2010: deep learning, the layered neural networks Geoffrey Hinton had spent a quarter of a century defending, and reinforcement learning, in which a program learns from the consequences of its own actions rather than from labelled examples, with ideas from neuroscience on top. The proving ground was games, because games have rules you can write down and scores you can read off the board. The first result, shown in 2013, was one agent that learned to play Atari games from the pixels alone. Google bought the company in 2014. In 2016 AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol in Seoul, and in 2017 its successor, AlphaZero, learned chess, shogi and Go from nothing but the rules and games against itself, with one algorithm, and beat the strongest existing program at each. Those are the three games in this article, in that order, and self-play is the loop I built. AlphaFold followed in 2020, then the predicted shapes of two hundred million proteins, then the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2024. Even the name is a triple nod: to deep learning, to Deep Blue, and to Deep Thought, the computer in *The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy* that was asked for the answer to everything.

Why am I reading it? Partly for the obvious reason: I work on AI platforms for a living and wanted the story of one of the architects of this revolution from the inside, and the book is exactly that and more. Partly because of the parallels, which kept catching me off guard: a games designer who smuggled a simulation into a theme park, a competitor who cannot pass a board game without wanting to win it, a man who thinks of the world as information and of the mind as something that builds reality rather than records it. I recognise more of that than is comfortable. And partly because of the belief. Hassabis believed in artificial intelligence when almost nobody did, with a conviction the book is honest enough to call close to religious, and he was right. There is a strand of transhumanism running through the story, from the Iain Banks novels he read at Bullfrog to the Singularity Summit where DeepMind found its first investor, and he keeps a dry British distance from the Californian version of it. I have a strand of my own, with a different spin and from a different direction, and that is a subject for another piece. It is enough to say here that I did not come to the book as a sceptic.

What hooked me in those early pages, more than the prodigy story, is how often games are the way in. Hassabis learns programming through chess. His first intelligent program plays Othello. At Cambridge he learns Go from a professor and takes shogi far enough to reach the top of the English rankings. His friend David Silver, who will later lead the AlphaGo work, finds his way into the field through a textbook on reinforcement learning, read in the south of France after their games company failed. Mallaby traces the thread back to Claude Shannon's 1950 paper on programming a computer to play chess, which Levy's handbook had introduced to the twelve-year-old. Shannon wrote that chess programs had no practical importance, but that mastering a game might serve as "a wedge in attacking other problems of a similar nature and of greater significance". That sentence is seventy-six years old and still the best one-line justification I know for spending a month on board games.

## My own games

My own chess is a smaller story. I joined a chess club in my early teens, played the regional tournaments, and did well in a few of them: nothing that would have sent a chess columnist across the hall to talk to my father, as one did for Hassabis when he was six, and nothing I would put in the same paragraph as his career if the book had not put the two of us in the same bookshop. But the game stayed. I do not turn down a game when one is offered; the last one was against a coworker and friend on Union Square in San Francisco, this year. I have a weakness for the big outdoor sets with knee-high pieces, and there are two I like, one in Lucerne and one beside the Rhine here in Basel. On trains I play on lichess on my phone. And I have enjoyed, more than I expected to, the odd second life the game found in the 2020s, when a television series about a fictional prodigy sent people out to buy boards and grandmasters turned into streamers with audiences no tournament hall could hold. I did not see that coming, and I am not complaining.

The other half of my gaming life is what German calls Aufbauspiele, the building games: Anno, Die Siedler, the whole tycoon genre, anything where you lay down a world with rules and watch it run. Hassabis's *Theme Park* is one of them, which made that chapter feel personal. The visitors who get thirsty when you oversalt the fries and buy more drinks, the riders who are sick when the coaster is too fast, are exactly the kind of mechanism I play these games for. I like games best when they try to mimic reality and let a thick ruleset generate stories nobody wrote, which is why I love Dwarf Fortress, and it is why I keep building simulations of my own, from [a dish of neurons](https://raskell.io/articles/brain-emulation-as-an-infrastructure-problem/) that learns under stimulation to [a terrarium](https://terrarium.raskell.io) left to evolve. A chess engine, seen from that side, is the smallest simulation worth building: a complete world with rules, and inside it an agent that has to learn.

## Why games, and why these three

Shannon's point is practical. A game like chess has rules you can write down completely, a result you can read off the board without argument, and a depth that no amount of study has exhausted. That combination is rare. Most real problems have fuzzy rules, contested outcomes and no yardstick. A game gives you a laboratory where a new idea can be tested in an afternoon, against centuries of human knowledge, and the answer is a number.

Chess, shogi and Go also happen to be the three games along which the history of this field unfolded, in that order, and each one broke what had worked on the one before. That is why I picked all three rather than one.

**Chess** came out of northern India around the sixth century as chaturanga, travelled through Persia into Europe, and took its modern form, with the long-range queen and bishop, in Spain and Italy at the end of the fifteenth century. It is the game Shannon chose, the game Levy's handbook teaches, and the one the classical method of search plus evaluation was built for. In 1997 IBM's Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov by searching two hundred million positions a second on purpose-built chips, with an evaluation written and tuned by people. It was a triumph of the three parts and a disappointment to anyone hoping for insight: the machine won by looking further, not by understanding more. The interesting question, from Levy's chapter onwards, was whether the evaluation function could be learned instead of written. For chess, that question was answered between 2018 and 2020 with a small neural network that lives inside the engine's inner loop. It is called NNUE, and it was not invented for chess.

**Shogi** is the Japanese branch of the same family. It arrived in Japan by way of China and Southeast Asia by the eleventh century, took its present form by the sixteenth, and became an institution under the Tokugawa shoguns, who put the best players on stipends; the first Meijin, the title that still crowns a shogi champion, was awarded in 1612. Today it is played by millions in Japan, with a professional system, televised title matches, and a young star, Sota Fujii, who in 2023, at twenty-one, held all eight major titles at once. The board is nine by nine, each side has twenty pieces of eight kinds, and most of them promote when they reach the far third of the board. One rule makes it a different game. A captured piece changes sides, goes into the captor's hand, and can later be dropped onto almost any empty square as a move. Nothing ever leaves the board for good, so the game never simplifies the way chess does. There are about eighty moves to choose from at a typical turn against chess's thirty-five, the games are longer, and the endgame is a mutual race rather than a technical grind. For a programmer, drops make the evaluation function much harder to write by hand, which is why the learning happened here first. Computer shogi was transformed in 2006 by Bonanza, the first program whose evaluation was fitted to professional games rather than tuned by hand. In 2017 Ponanza beat the reigning Meijin, Amahiko Sato, and in 2018 Yu Nasu published the network design that Stockfish adopted for chess two years later. Shogi is where the idea I was chasing came from.

**Go** is older than both and simpler than either. It comes from China, where it is at least two and a half thousand years old and was counted among the four accomplishments of a cultivated person alongside music, calligraphy and painting; it reached Japan by the eighth century, where the Edo-period houses of professional players were funded by the shogunate, and it has deep roots in Korea, where it is called baduk. The rules fit on a card. Two players alternately place black and white stones on the intersections of a nineteen-by-nineteen grid. A group of stones with no empty points next to it is captured and removed. At the end, whoever surrounds more of the board wins, with a few points' compensation to white for moving second. From those rules comes a game with around two hundred and fifty choices at every turn, games of two or three hundred moves, and positions that nobody has been able to score by hand. Levy's three parts fail here. A search that looks four moves ahead in Go sees almost nothing, and there is no formula for who is winning to apply at the leaves. Go was the game that everyone in the field, including Hassabis, called the grand challenge, and it was the one DeepMind chose when it wanted to show what it had. The programs of the late 2000s had replaced the chess method with Monte Carlo tree search, which plays thousands of random games out to the end and counts who wins; that got to strong-amateur level and stuck. AlphaGo kept that search and gave it two neural networks, one to suggest moves and one to judge positions, trained first on human games and then on its own, and in March 2016 it beat Lee Sedol four games to one.

So: one game where the classical method works and the network replaces the evaluation; one where the same method strains and the network was invented; one where the method fails and the network has to guide the search itself. The three together are a short course in forty years of the field, and each one can be measured against opponents anyone can download.

## Why I built it rather than read about it

Hassabis likes to cite Feynman's line about not understanding what you cannot build, and it is the honest reason for this project. I have read the AlphaGo paper and the Stockfish NNUE write-ups more than once. I could explain the diagrams. I could not have told you what K is, or why a network that wins at equal search depth can lose at equal time, or how many hours of a laptop's life a generation of self-play costs, because those are the things the papers leave out and the only way to learn them is to pay for them. Reading the book made the gap uncomfortable, and the same itch that makes me build terrariums wanted the world with the rules and the learner inside it running on my own machine.

The other reason is that the ingredients are, for the first time, all on my desk. The ideas are published and the reference implementations are open source. The laptop is a MacBook Pro with an Apple M4, ten cores and sixteen gigabytes of memory, which is not a research machine and has more general computing power than Deep Blue had. The browser on my phone can now run compiled code with vector instructions and real threads. And the writing of the code itself, which would have been a winter of evenings, took days with a coding agent, with me deciding what to build and the agent typing most of it. That belongs in the method: the agent wrote code, a match between two engines decided whether the code was any good, and the match does not care who wrote it.

## Why Rust, and not PyTorch

The obvious way to do machine learning in 2026 is Python and PyTorch, and if the goal had been a model that answers questions on a server, that is what I would have used. The goal was an opponent on my phone, in a browser tab, offline, and that changed everything downstream.

A chess evaluation is called inside the search, about a million times a second, on one core, with no batching, rather than once per request. A network that lives there cannot be a model behind an API. It has to be a few hundred lines of arithmetic in the engine's own language, run on integers, and updated incrementally as moves are made rather than recomputed from scratch, which is the whole trick of NNUE. The inference, in other words, had to be hand-written anyway. Once it was, the trainer was the same arithmetic run backwards, over a million parameters and inputs that are almost all zero, and it fitted in a few hundred lines too. Writing it is also how I found out what the framework would have hidden from me: the one constant I guessed instead of fitting turned a winning network into a losing one, and I would not have known why.

Rust is the language I write everything on this site in, from the [neuron culture](https://hotaru.raskell.io) to the [fantasy console](https://wasmad.raskell.io), and it is the right tool for an engine for the usual reasons: no garbage collector in a loop that runs a million times a second, control over memory layout, and a compiler that produces WebAssembly with vector instructions from the same source as the native binary. One language runs from the self-play games on the laptop to the move on the phone, in one repository, and the web app has no build step. The trade-off is honest too. Training a small, sparse network on the CPU is fine. If the Go network ends up as a convolutional net with millions of dense parameters, Rust on ten cores will be slow, and I will have to decide whether to write a Metal kernel or admit that this is where the laptop study meets a GPU.

## Why WebAssembly

Because the phone is the point. An opponent that lives on a server is not mine; an opponent in an app store is somebody else's to approve. A web page that I add to my home screen, that works on a plane, and that runs the identical binary to the one on my laptop is the version I wanted, and in 2026 the browser can do it. WebAssembly has had 128-bit vector instructions for a while, and Safari now lets a page share memory between threads if it is served with the right isolation headers, so the chess engine on my phone searches on four cores. Lichess, the free chess site, runs Stockfish the same way for its analysis board, which was my proof that the approach was sound before I started.

The constraint also shaped the design more than any paper did. A network that has to be downloaded with the page and run on a phone has to be small; Kishi's chess network is 820 kilobytes and is compiled into the engine binary. A search that has to run in a browser tab has to be frugal. Every decision that looks like taste in the code is really the phone saying no to something.

## What happened

The chess engine came first: bitboards, a search with the usual family of pruning heuristics, and a hand-written evaluation borrowed from a well-known set of piece-square tables. Against Stockfish configured the way lichess configures its computer opponents, with twenty games a level on one core, it beats level 4 nineteen games to one, beats level 6 thirteen to seven, and loses to level 7 nineteen and a half to a half. If you have played the lichess computer, that places it: a solid club player, nowhere near the top.

Then the loop. The engine played itself from random openings for fifty-two minutes, which produced 5.6 million positions from fifty-seven thousand games, each labelled with what the search thought of it and how the game ended. A network trained on those positions in under twenty minutes beat the hand-written evaluation it replaced by 85 rating points, plus or minus 32, when both sides were allowed the same number of positions to look at. When both sides were allowed the same number of milliseconds, they came out even, because the network costs two and a half times as much per position. That is the whole problem of this kind of learning in one sentence, and I did not understand it before I had the numbers.

Shogi got its own engine with the same shape and a hand-written evaluation, which beats Fairy-Stockfish's weakest setting twenty games to none and loses to a middling one eighteen to two. Go got the method of the late 2000s, Monte Carlo tree search with the shape patterns from the old MoGo program, and against GNU Go at its lowest level, with a second a move, it wins three games in ten. All three play on the phone. The chess one is the only one I would call a satisfying opponent at the top levels, and that is with the hand-written evaluation, because the trained network has not yet earned its place on the clock.

## What this opened up

I started with one question, whether I could build Levy's three parts, and I have ended the month with five better ones.

The chess network wins at equal search and draws at equal time. Does that change after more generations of self-play, as the games it learns from get stronger, or is a laptop-sized network always going to be paying for its own cost? The loop is running as I write this, at low priority, so the laptop stays usable. Why did one constant swing the result by 176 rating points, and what does that say about the contract between a learned component and the hand-tuned system it plugs into? Does the same loop work for shogi once the network can see where the kings are, which is what Nasu's original design did and mine does not yet? Go needs the second kind of loop, where the search teaches the network which moves to look at, and I do not know what a laptop can train on a full nineteen-by-nineteen board; the AlphaGo chapters of the book, which I am about to reach, will tell me what it took in 2016, and I want to know what it takes in 2026 on a machine from a shop. And underneath all of it: how much of an engine's strength survives the trip from a native binary to a browser tab on a phone, and what threads buy back.

Each of those is a few days of work and a few numbers, and I have started keeping [a notebook](https://github.com/raskell-io/kishi/blob/main/docs/study/notebook.md) in the repository so that the numbers are written down as they arrive, failures included. If the answers turn out to be as interesting as the questions, this may become the first of several pieces, one idea at a time, chess first, then shogi, then Go. Let's see.

author: Raffael Schneider
date: 2026-10-25
description: "Urbanisation was miserable for the people who lived through it and better for everyone who came after. The argument about AI and work has the same shape."
tags: [history-of-technology, cities, future-of-work, social-reform, world-history]
---

# The move to the city

The comparison I keep coming back to is the move from the land to the city. The industrial cities of the nineteenth century were dense, dirty and short of everything, sanitation first of all; people got sick in them and died in them. The people still on the land did not want to go, and thought life was better where they were, and for them, in their own lifetimes, it often was. Over generations the move made almost everyone better off, and nobody now argues for going back; the long series is on Our World in Data's page on urbanisation, below.

The thinking today has the same shape. The fear of what AI does to work is legitimate on the timescale of a life, and the long-run reading, that a [democratised capability](https://raskell.io/notes/a-capability-democratised/) ends up better for everyone collectively, is probably also right. Both can be true, and the part that history does not make comfortable is the middle: [the tumult in between](https://raskell.io/notes/the-tumult-in-between/).

## References

- Our World in Data, [Urbanization](https://ourworldindata.org/urbanization): the share of people living in cities over two centuries, by country.

# Ideas stop waiting

I have been shipping more this year than in any year before, and the honest explanation is that nothing changed in me. What changed is that the ideas I had carried in the back of my head for years, project ideas, research questions, things I had never properly put into words, now have a way out. [Kishi](https://raskell.io/articles/learning-to-play/) is one: three game engines and a training loop, which would have been a winter of evenings, done in a month beside a day job. [The handbook](https://raskell.io/series/the-agent-platform-handbook/) is another, and what a working day looks like with the agents in it is in [How I Work These Days](https://raskell.io/articles/how-i-work-these-days/).

I am not faster at the things I already did. A whole category of things has moved from some day to this weekend, and the limiting factor is now how clearly I can say what I want. It feels like a once-in-a-lifetime window, and I think it is one, for a reason I set out in [the window before the utility](https://raskell.io/notes/the-window-before-the-utility/). There is a word for what the window gives a person, and I have come round to it: [power, in the good sense](https://raskell.io/notes/power-in-the-good-sense/).

title: "The tumult in between"
url: https://raskell.io/notes/the-tumult-in-between/
author: Raffael Schneider
date: 2026-10-25
description: "If AI ends in post-scarcity, the dangerous part is the interval: jobs going before goods become nearly free, with no agreed idea of where the ship steers."
tags: [post-scarcity, future-of-work, economics, risk, social-reform, policy, abundance]
---

# The tumult in between

The two answers people reach for are both answers to the end state. Universal basic income is the money-focused one: if the economy produces enough, pay everyone a floor. Basic access to goods and services is the resource-focused one: if things become nearly free, guarantee the things rather than the money. Each has its advocates and each frightens a lot of people, and neither says anything about the interval. The question is older than AI: Theodor Hertzka's *Freeland* and *Das soziale Problem*, which I have read, are a nineteenth-century design for a society where access to land and capital is guaranteed rather than earned, and the distance between the book and any attempt to live it is the interval I mean.

The interval is the part I cannot see through. If AI really does lead to something like a post-scarcity economy, where most things are virtually free, the jobs go first and the abundance comes later, and in between there is a stretch where people lose their livelihoods at scale with nothing yet in place, and no shared view of where the collective ship is steering. That stretch will be chaotic, and I do not know how long it is. [The move to the city](https://raskell.io/notes/the-move-to-the-city/) says such intervals end well; it does not say they are short. The most constructive response to it I have heard is [citizen entrepreneurs](https://raskell.io/notes/citizen-entrepreneurs/).

## References

- Basic Income Earth Network, [About basic income](https://basicincome.org/about-basic-income/): the definition and the main arguments, from the people who have made the case longest.

# A capability, democratised

Making software used to be reserved for people with a particular privilege: the money to pay a team, or the team itself, or the years it takes to learn to program well enough to build something real. [The power](https://raskell.io/notes/power-in-the-good-sense/) I wrote about is that privilege, democratised. Anyone with an idea, a subscription, and the patience to describe what they want can now have it built, and the ones who learn to describe well get a great deal.

Democratised capabilities have a history, and the history has a shape. Nobody who built the printing press or the web could say what people would do with them, and what people did was not on anyone's plan. The web's version of that story is in [The Web Was the Training Set](https://raskell.io/articles/the-web-was-the-training-set/): a protocol given away, and thirty years of uses nobody at CERN drew. It emerged, from millions of small decisions, and it was better for almost everyone, collectively and in the end, even where it was hard for the people in the middle of it. I expect the same of this, with the same caveat; [the move to the city](https://raskell.io/notes/the-move-to-the-city/) is the comparison I keep returning to. And I expect the window in which it is an advantage rather than a baseline to be short, for the reason in [the window before the utility](https://raskell.io/notes/the-window-before-the-utility/).

---
title: "Power, in the good sense"
url: https://raskell.io/notes/power-in-the-good-sense/
author: Raffael Schneider
date: 2026-10-25
description: "The right word for what AI gives an individual builder is power, meant as capability rather than domination. It is refreshing to say so."
tags: [augmentation, democratisation, ai-engineering, ethics]
---

# Power, in the good sense

The word I have settled on for the feeling in [ideas stop waiting](https://raskell.io/notes/ideas-stop-waiting/) is power. Not in the sense the word usually carries, power over someone, but in the plain sense: being capable of doing something, having possibilities, having a moat of your own. Through the AI services anyone can subscribe to, we became powerful.

It is an uncomfortable choice of word at first, and the longer I sit with it the more I like it. We have trained ourselves to hear power only as hierarchy, and to look for a victim in every arrangement that has some. This is a kind of power nobody took from anyone. It was not redistributed; it was created, and handed out to whoever cared to learn it. Capability is power, and it is a relief to say so without apology. It is the capability of one person directing many hands, which is what [sixteen agents under one manager](https://raskell.io/articles/what-sixteen-ai-agents-taught-me-about-management/) turned out to be about. What makes it more than a personal feeling is that the capability is [democratised](https://raskell.io/notes/a-capability-democratised/), which is where the interesting consequences start.


================================================================================

---
title: "The window before the utility"
url: https://raskell.io/notes/the-window-before-the-utility/
author: Raffael Schneider
date: 2026-10-25
description: "Tokens will be a metered utility and AI as ordinary as electricity. Until then, learning to use it well is an advantage that will not come around again."
tags: [inference, economics, augmentation, democratisation, ai-engineering, energy]
---

# The window before the utility

I argued in [The Economics of Inference](https://raskell.io/articles/the-economics-of-inference/) that tokens are a metered utility, priced per unit like water or electricity, and that pricing and provision will converge on the utility model. The consequence follows: AI capability will be commoditised. It will become normal, boring, and available to everyone on the same terms, and once it is, having it is no advantage at all, any more than having electricity is. The model behind it becomes a dependency like any other, the argument of [The Model Is a Dependency](https://raskell.io/articles/the-model-is-a-dependency/), and its bill gets metered into the loop, as in [The Bill Is Part of the Loop](https://raskell.io/articles/the-bill-is-part-of-the-loop/).

That is the end state. We are not there. The models, the tools and the prices are still moving every quarter, and in a moving market the advantage goes to the people who adopt early and learn to use the thing well, which is work. This is why the feeling in [ideas stop waiting](https://raskell.io/notes/ideas-stop-waiting/) is a window and not a new normal: nobody in 2036 will write a note about feeling empowered by their electricity supply. The window is open now, it is once in a lifetime in the literal sense, and what one does with it is the question. One answer is in [citizen entrepreneurs](https://raskell.io/notes/citizen-entrepreneurs/).


================================================================================

---
title: "Citizen entrepreneurs"
url: https://raskell.io/notes/citizen-entrepreneurs/
author: Raffael Schneider
date: 2026-10-25
description: "My friend's answer to the transition: with AI, ordinary people can find a business opportunity, build the business, and run it. He built an idea factory."
tags: [entrepreneurship, democratisation, future-of-work, agents, augmentation, factories]
---

# Citizen entrepreneurs

A friend of mine, an enterprise architect at a large Swiss energy group, answers [the tumult in between](https://raskell.io/notes/the-tumult-in-between/) with the observation that the same tools that threaten jobs make citizen entrepreneurs possible. An ordinary person can use AI to identify a business opportunity, use AI to build the business, and use AI to operate it. The barrier was never only money; it was the ten different competences a business needs on day one, and those are now available by the hour. The operating half is already true for infrastructure, where one person can now run what used to take a team, as I argued in [How AI Makes Bare Metal Viable Again](https://raskell.io/articles/how-ai-makes-bare-metal-viable-again/). He took his own idea seriously enough to build a business idea factory, a system that generates and evaluates opportunities. About a week before we talked, someone else announced a project with the same shape on Hacker News, which he took as confirmation rather than competition.

I find it the most hopeful reading of [the window](https://raskell.io/notes/the-window-before-the-utility/), and the one with the most work in it. It assumes the capability really is [democratised](https://raskell.io/notes/a-capability-democratised/), which I believe, and it assumes people will take it up, which is the part the window is for.

title: "The Web Was the Training Set"
url: https://raskell.io/articles/the-web-was-the-training-set/
author: Raffael Schneider
date: 2026-10-24
description: "Tim Berners-Lee's memoir is the story of a British engineer at a Franco-Swiss lab giving a protocol away. Read in 2026, it is also the origin story of AI's data supply."
tags: [history-of-technology, hypertext, training-data, data-sovereignty, research-labs, intellectual-property, europe]
