review_of: "This Is for Everyone"
review_of_author: "Tim Berners-Lee"
review_of_kind: book
review_of_year: 2025
rating: 8/10
---

# The Web Was the Training Set

## In short

Tim Berners-Lee's *This Is for Everyone* is a memoir, a history of the web and a manifesto for data sovereignty, and its last line, that the web provided the data for AI, is its real thesis. The book is strongest as geography, showing the web came out of CERN and Switzerland, and that releasing it into the public domain was right while Europe had no plan for what came after. The web worked as a corpus because of its design: documents with stable addresses, marked-up text and explicit links, so the commons was the dataset before anyone called it one. I add a consequence the book does not reach: what was never put on the web is not in the models, which is why European archives and records hold the next increment of quality. Solid pods make the data yours but not the agent yours; I give the book 8 out of 10 for first-rate history, an important AI idea left undeveloped, and Solid chapters that read like a prospectus.

I read *This Is for Everyone* on the shore in Okinawa in the autumn of 2025 and wrote about it that winter in [Looking back on 2025](https://raskell.io/articles/looking-back-on-2025/). That piece was about reefs and the open web. This one is about a sentence I read past the first time and cannot get out of my head a year later, after twelve months of building agent platforms for a living. It is the last line of the last chapter: "AI had aced the Imitation Game, and the web provided the data that made it possible."

Berners-Lee writes it as a coda. I think it is the thesis of the book, and I think he undersells it.

## What the book is

Three books share the binding. The first is a memoir: a boy in East Sheen whose parents wrote code for the Ferranti Mark 1 and knew Alan Turing, physics at Oxford, a homebrew computer built from factory-reject transistors and an adding machine fished out of a skip at a timber yard, a first job at Plessey in Poole. The second is the history everyone buys the book for: CERN, the 1989 memo, the NeXT cube, the first server, Mosaic, the World Wide Web Consortium. The third is a manifesto for the next thirty years: data sovereignty, Solid pods, and an AI that works for you rather than for the company that trained it. Stephen Witt, who wrote *The Thinking Machine* about Nvidia, is the co-author, and the prose is clean. The structure is looser. The book proceeds by association, which suits its subject, and which is also why some reviewers found it shapeless.

Compressed into one argument: the web won because it was universal and free, both qualities are now being eroded from the inside, and the way out is to give people control of their own data so that the next layer, the agents, works for them. I think he would accept that summary.

## The epicentre was not where you expect

The book is strongest as geography. The web did not come out of Silicon Valley, and Berners-Lee is careful to say he barely knew the place existed when he graduated. In 1977, he writes, no Silicon Valley recruiter came to Oxford. His computing education came from his parents, from Manchester by way of Ferranti, and from the strange luck of being born in 1955, the year after Turing died, into a house with the Mark 1's punch tape on the floor.

Switzerland comes before CERN. His first job abroad was in Zug, writing microprocessor code for a wafer saw, and he dates his attachment to the country to a night of Kaffee Fertig in a chalet above the cows: "I think it was then that I first fell in love with Switzerland. I'm still in love with it today." CERN follows, first as a six-month contract in 1980 and then as a fellowship from 1984, with an apartment in Saint-Genis across the French border and windsurfing on the lake. The web was conceived in that corridor, at the coffee counter where people from twenty countries worked out how to run a machine nobody fully understood. The 1989 memo says so in its first argument: "CERN is a model in miniature of the rest of the world in a few years' time. CERN meets now some problems which the rest of the world will have to face soon."

What I had forgotten is how precarious the whole thing was. The question that hung over the project, in his own phrasing, was "Why, exactly, is the European taxpayer financing the oddball passion project of a thirty-six-year-old computer programmer in the Data and Documents division of a Franco-Swiss particle physics laboratory?" The answer, for three years, was that two managers, Mike Sendall and Peggie Rimmer, chose to hide him from the budget. Sendall's pencilled "vague, but exciting" on the memo is famous. The chapter around it, about Sendall's illness and the marriage Peggie entered to be able to care for him in a Swiss hospital, is the most human thing in the book, and it is a reminder that infrastructure gets built because particular people protect it for a while.

The British bookend is the 2012 Olympics, where Danny Boyle asked him to type the title phrase on a NeXT in front of 80,000 people as one of the inventions "Britons had shared with the world." Between Geneva and London there is the one scene I would put in every history of computing: the 1992 NeXT developer conference in Paris, where Berners-Lee set up the web on a folding table to show Steve Jobs, and an aide pulled Jobs away one table early. He calls it a sliding-doors moment. I think he is right, and I think the door that closed was a European one. Two years later the consortium went to MIT, with a foothold at INRIA. The centre of gravity followed the money.

## Free, because Gopher was not

The chapter I would make mandatory reading for anyone who writes policy about open standards is the one about Gopher. Until 1994 more people used Gopher than the web. In February 1993 the University of Minnesota announced that it reserved the right to charge licensees. It never collected a cent, by his account, and the announcement alone killed the protocol within months.

Berners-Lee's reaction is the part that matters. He realised the web was in the same position: written on CERN machines, on a CERN salary, owned by CERN. "For the web to succeed, it had to be free." Inside the lab there was a faction, he calls them "patriots", who wanted the opposite: spin the web out as a company "to prove that Europe could compete" with Silicon Valley. He was sympathetic and overruled them. On 30 April 1993 CERN's directors signed a statement that "CERN relinquishes all intellectual property rights to this code, both source and binary and permission is given to anyone to use, duplicate, modify and distribute it."

I agree with the decision and I want to be exact about what it cost. Europe funded the research, hosted the invention, and gave away the result without keeping an institution that could compound on it. The protocol stayed free; the platforms built on top of it did not, and none of the large ones are European. That pattern, the commons funded here and captured there, is the background to the argument I made in [The Bottleneck Is Data, and Europe Is Sitting on It](https://raskell.io/articles/the-bottleneck-is-data-and-europe-is-sitting-on-it/), and reading this chapter again made me more convinced of it, not less. The public-domain release was correct. The absence of any European plan for what came after was the mistake, and it was not his to make.

## The web was the training set

Now the sentence. Berners-Lee's own account of machine learning is short and, for a man who spent two decades on the semantic web, generous. Machine learning, he writes, "has three legs: software, hardware and data," and "it is the third leg, the data, that is in many cases the missing piece of the puzzle." He tells the GPT story with the detail I had not registered: the first GPT trained on a corpus of self-published romance and science fiction, and "its output was closer to nonsense than meaningful human prose." The models became useful only once OpenAI turned to the non-profit archivists at Common Crawl and trained on the web itself. His conclusion, in the chapter on intelligent machines: "Data was the fuel for this breakthrough" and, specifically, free and open web data.

The numbers back him. In the GPT-3 paper, filtered Common Crawl is 410 billion tokens and 60 per cent of the training mix by weight; the rest is more web (WebText2), two book corpora, and Wikipedia, which is also the web. The 2024 PNAS study he cites as the Turing Test being passed found that a GPT-4 model's choices in behavioural games were statistically indistinguishable from a random person drawn from tens of thousands of human subjects in more than fifty countries. Whatever one thinks of the framing, the mechanism is not in dispute. The models learned to write from what people had published, and people had published it because of the thing this book describes.

What I want to add is why the web worked as a corpus, because the reasons are design decisions in chapters 2 and 3, not accidents. A page is a document with a stable address. Text is marked up, so titles and headings and lists can be told apart. Links are explicit, so relevance can be computed; PageRank is a graph algorithm over anchor tags, and Common Crawl's filters and deduplication lean on the same structure. The hash sign, the place where in his words networking and hypertext "meet", is also where a crawler learns which part of an address is a document and which is a position inside it. He describes the five-star ladder for open government data later in the book: on the web, structured, non-proprietary, addressable, linked. The web as a whole climbed that ladder without being asked, and a quarter of a century of people exposing their writing to each other in a structured, addressable form is what a transformer was eventually pointed at. The commons was the dataset before anyone called it one.

Two consequences follow, and the book reaches the first but not the second.

The first is his. The same openness that let the web grow is why the text could be taken without asking. He is blunt that Common Crawl "contains a lot of copyrighted material" and that the models can reproduce it, and he lands on a position I did not expect from the man who refused to patent HTTP: "An AI should only have the right to use your creative work as input if you have explicitly opted in, and should you opt in, you have a right to get paid." He proposes a Content ID for text and admits the attribution problem is unsolved, with a GPT-4 ode to a dishwasher in the style of Philip Larkin as the test case. Nothing in it is Larkin's, and all of it is. This site, for what it is worth, publishes a Content-Signal line in its `robots.txt` and a `llms.txt` and asks for attribution, which is roughly his opt-in with the terms attached. Whether anyone reads it is a separate question.

The second is mine. If the web was the training set, then what was never put on the web is not in the models. That is the whole of the European data argument in one line. The archives, the press runs, the parliamentary records, the century of paywalled newspaper pages, the scientific proceedings in twenty-four languages, exist in machine-readable form or could, and sit outside the corpus the frontier models were built from. Berners-Lee's own life makes the point: the data at CERN only became valuable to physics once his system put it where other people could find it, and the same is true of the data Europe is sitting on now. The next increment of model quality is not in a larger crawl of the same web. It is in the material the web never got.

Where I disagree with him is on the mechanism of intelligence. He argues that scale settles the question: feed a model "a high proportion of all the sentences in the whole world" and "it builds a network with the number of nodes comparable to the number of neurons in your brain." Parameters are not neurons and the comparison is loose; I read it as enthusiasm, not as a claim he would defend at a whiteboard. He also makes the stronger philosophical claim that there is no difference between simulating consciousness and having it. He is entitled to that view, and I would have liked a chapter on it rather than a paragraph.

## Engineering lore

The chapters on the first year of the web are the most fun for anyone who ships software, and they are honest about regret in a way founders rarely are. The URL, in his account, was "the most important thing I ever wrote", a few lines of code that reduced the friction of moving between machines to a click. The rule for the whole design was to reuse what people already knew: SGML for the markup, DNS for the names, Apollo workstation paths for the addressing. The double slash came from Apollo, and he apologises for it. The DNS order came from the United States, and he wishes he had used the British convention, most general part first, so that addresses read `uk.co.widgets.www`. The read-write browser he built on the NeXT, where every page was editable, lost to read-only browsers because users preferred one tool for reading and another for writing, and the web became "a lot more passive" than he intended. Marc Andreessen added the `IMG` tag to Mosaic unilaterally while the argument about a more general design was still running, which is exactly what a public-domain standard permits. The whole first browser, editor and all, was 9,555 lines of Objective-C.

There is a sentence in there for people who build platforms: "software designers, like urban planners, make the mistake of demanding that the user acts like the system, rather than the other way around." The system behind the web is rigidly modernist, he says; the web on top of it was designed to be an anarchic jumble. Most of the platforms I have seen fail did so by letting the first layer leak into the second.

## Charlie, and who the agent works for

The last third of the book is about Solid, the protocol for personal data pods that Berners-Lee has been building since the semantic web years, and about Inrupt, the company he co-founded to commercialise it. The argument runs through a 2017 dialogue with an imagined assistant called Charlie. Charlie reads a chef's cookbooks as a training set to reconstruct a dish, invests in a start-up to give Bob something in common with his mother-in-law, and when asked who it works for answers: "Legally, ethically and algorithmically, I work for you, Bob." It was written before ChatGPT, and it reads now like a product spec for the agents everyone is building.

As someone who builds the other side of that spec, I think he has the problem right and the solution only half right. The problem is real: the apps on a phone do not share data because they do not trust each other and do not speak the same language, and the agent that gets access to everything is the one that most needs to be trustworthy. That is the point of a context layer, which I have argued is [the product](https://raskell.io/articles/context-is-the-product/) and [a write path](https://raskell.io/articles/memory-is-a-write-path/), not a cache. Pods are a reasonable place to put that layer. They say nothing about who runs the model that reads it, where the inference happens, or what the agent is allowed to do with what it reads, and that is where the agent platforms I work on spend most of their effort. A pod makes the data yours. It does not make the agent yours.

The Solid chapters also read like a pitch, which they are, and Publishers Weekly's complaint that the scheme "sounds fuzzy and dull" in his telling is fair. The ideas are not dull. The telling is, because it is written from inside the company. I would have cut a third of it.

## Verdict

I give it 8 out of 10. The history is first-rate and told by the one person who can tell it, with the Swiss and British years given their due and the Gopher chapter alone worth the price. The AI chapters contain the most important idea in the book, that the web is the reason the models exist, and then leave it to the reader to work out what follows. The Solid chapters are a prospectus. The structure wanders, and the forecast is thin next to the history; John Arlidge in *The Times* called it 400 pages with no driving narrative, which is harsh and not entirely wrong.

Read it if you build anything on the web or on models trained from it, and read it for the history first. You do not need a technical background; the hardest idea in the book is the hash sign, and he explains it in a paragraph. Pair it with Mallaby's *The Infinity Machine*, which I am reading now and which picks up the Hassabis thread this book opens at a Google dinner in 2014. And read the last line again when you are done. He provided the data. The question of what we do with the rest of it is still open, and it is a European question more than he lets on.

# Opus 5.5 is the best Opus since 4.5

| | Opus 4.5 | Opus 5.5 |
|---|---|---|
| Released | 24 November 2025 | 22 September 2026 |
| Price per million tokens, input / output | $5 / $25 | $4 / $20 |
| Fast mode | not offered | $8 / $40 |
| Context window | 200K | 1M |
| Model ID | `claude-opus-4-5-20251101` | `claude-opus-5-5` |

Opus 4.5 was the moment Claude Code started working the way it was meant to. I had paid for Claude Code since May 2025 without being convinced; over the 2025 Christmas break, with Opus 4.5, it carried whole projects, and I built [Zentinel](https://zentinelproxy.io) with it. I wrote that up in [How I Work These Days](https://raskell.io/articles/how-i-work-these-days/) and [What Sixteen AI Agents Taught Me About Management](https://raskell.io/articles/what-sixteen-ai-agents-taught-me-about-management/), and it is the opening of my [Basel talk](https://raskell.io/talks/iat-13-basel/).

Opus 5.5 is the first release since then that felt like the same kind of step rather than an increment.

- **It holds the thread.** Long sessions that span a theme, a site, CI, and several data files stay coherent. The search across this site, the reading log, and the agent-readable files behind them were built in sessions with it.
- **Speed changes how I work with it.** Fast enough that I stay in the loop instead of switching away while it runs. Fast mode exists for when that matters more than the bill.
- **The cost moved the right way.** A cheaper rate card than 4.5, and Anthropic puts it at about 40 per cent cheaper to run than Opus 5 on typical work. The rate card is half the story; fewer wasted turns is the other half, the same argument I made in [The Economics of Inference](https://raskell.io/articles/the-economics-of-inference/).
- **Opus is the default again.** For most of my work I no longer pick a smaller model to save money, which was the point of 4.5 too.

What I do not know yet: whether it holds up on the hardest, longest-running tasks, where the gap to a larger model would show first. A month is not a benchmark.

Sources: [Introducing Claude Opus 4.5](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-opus-4-5), [Introducing Claude Opus 5.5](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-opus-5-5), [Opus 5.5 model overview](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/opus-5-5/overview).

title: "Observability Is Not Logging"
url: https://raskell.io/articles/observability-is-not-logging/
author: Raffael Schneider
date: 2026-10-20
description: "A cost total says nothing about how a run went. This part turns each agent run into a trace: which turn escalated, which tool failed, where the money went."
tags: [agents, ai-platforms, observability, opentelemetry, typescript]
series: the-agent-platform-handbook
---

# Observability Is Not Logging

## In short

A cost total says nothing about how a run went; observability means being able to reconstruct what the system did, and for an agent that requires traces, not flat logs. The unit of an agent is the turn, and a run is a tree of spans: a small tracer treats runs and turns as nested scopes and model and tool calls as leaves, so parallel tools stay siblings. Tracing wraps the model interface and tool dispatch as decorators, so the loop barely changes, and the example trace shows most of the bill came from one escalation's cache write. When you need storage, queries or a UI, swap in OpenTelemetry behind the same calls and use the GenAI conventions, while expecting their experimental attribute names to shift. Do not put full prompts on spans, sample at the tail rather than the head, and remember that a trace shows what happened but not whether the run was correct.

> Part 9 of *The Agent Platform Handbook. From Loop to Platform.* Previous: [The Bill Is Part of the Loop](https://raskell.io/articles/the-bill-is-part-of-the-loop/). Next: Evaluation Closes the Loop.

[Post eight](https://raskell.io/articles/the-bill-is-part-of-the-loop/) taught the loop to read its own bill. Every response carries a `usage` object, a price table turns it into dollars, and a ledger accumulates the total, attributed to the run that caused it. The harness sits at tag [`post-08`](https://github.com/raskell-io/the-agent-platform-handbook/tree/post-08): a loop, a router, a fallback chain, a meter, and a budget that degrades before it stops.

That ledger can tell you a run cost forty cents across nine turns. It cannot tell you anything about the nine turns. Which one escalated to the strong model. Which tool call failed and got retried. Where the seven seconds of wall-clock actually went. The number is a sum, and a sum throws away the shape of the thing it summed.

This post keeps the number and recovers the shape. It turns the per-turn record the meter already produces into a trace: a tree of spans you can read top to bottom and see the run happen. The code is at tag [`post-09`](https://github.com/raskell-io/the-agent-platform-handbook/tree/post-09) of the companion repository.

## What observability actually meant

The word did not start in software. It came from control theory, where a system is observable if you can reconstruct its internal state from its outputs. That is the useful definition to carry into an agent harness, because it draws a line most "observability" tooling ignores. Logging gives you outputs. Observability is the claim that the outputs are enough to reconstruct what the system did.

The industry arrived here the long way. First there were logs, lines of text you grepped after something broke. Then metrics, counters and gauges you could graph, good for "how many" and useless for "which one." Then, in 2010, Google published Dapper, the paper that described distributed tracing: propagate an identifier across service boundaries, record a span for each unit of work, and reassemble the spans into the tree of a single request. Honeycomb and Charity Majors later reframed the whole category around a sharper test. Monitoring answers the questions you knew to ask in advance. Observability is for the questions you did not, the unknown-unknowns you can only investigate after the incident, by slicing the raw events along a dimension you did not think mattered until now.

OpenTelemetry is where that history settled. It defines three signal types, and the distinction between two of them is the entire point of this post. A log is an event at a point in time. A trace is a causal tree of spans, each with a start, an end, a parent, and attributes. Logs tell you what happened. Traces tell you what happened *because of* what, and how long each step took inside the whole.

An agent run is a distributed system that happens to live in one process. The loop calls the model, the model asks for tools, the tools call the filesystem and the network and sometimes another model. That is a call tree with latency and cost at every node. Logging it gives you a flat wall of lines in arrival order. Tracing it gives you the tree.

## The unit is the turn, the run is a tree

One reframe makes the code obvious. The atom of an agent is not the request and not the log line. It is the turn: one pass through the loop, one model call, zero or more tool calls, and whatever the model decided to do with the results. A run is a sequence of turns, and each turn is itself a small tree of work.

The meter from post eight was already emitting one structured record per model call. Input tokens, output tokens, cache reads, cost. Those records are not logs. They are span attributes that have not been given a span yet. All that is missing is the causal structure: a parent for each record, a start and an end, and the tool calls sitting as siblings to the model call inside the same turn.

So the job is not to add logging. The harness is drowning in potential log lines already. The job is to give the events a tree.

## A span in one type

A span is a named interval with attributes and children. That is the whole data structure.

```typescript
type SpanKind = "run" | "turn" | "model" | "tool";

type Span = {
  name: string;
  kind: SpanKind;
  startedAt: number;
  endedAt?: number;
  attributes: Record<string, string | number | boolean>;
  children: Span[];
  error?: string;
};
```

A tracer keeps track of which span is currently open, so that a new span becomes a child of it. The obvious design is a stack: push on start, pop on end, and the parent is whatever sits on top. That works for runs and turns, which happen one after another. It breaks on tools. Since [post three](https://raskell.io/articles/tools-how-agents-actually-do-things/), the tool calls of one turn run in parallel, and with a single stack the second call would land inside the first, as if one tool had called the other.

So the tracer separates the two cases. Runs and turns are scopes: `enter` opens one and pushes it, `exit` closes it and pops it. Model and tool calls are leaves: `start` attaches them under the current scope without pushing anything, so any number of them can be open at once.

```typescript
class Tracer {
  root?: Span;
  private open: Span[] = [];

  enter(name: string, kind: SpanKind, attributes = {}): Span {
    const span = this.start(name, kind, attributes);
    this.open.push(span);
    return span;
  }

  exit(span: Span, error?: string) {
    this.end(span, error);
    this.open.pop();
  }

  start(name: string, kind: SpanKind, attributes = {}): Span {
    const span: Span = { name, kind, startedAt: now(), attributes, children: [] };
    const parent = this.open[this.open.length - 1];
    if (parent) parent.children.push(span);
    else this.root = span;
    return span;
  }

  end(span: Span, error?: string) {
    span.endedAt = now();
    if (error) span.error = error;
  }
}
```

`now()` is `performance.now()`, a monotonic clock rather than wall time, so a clock adjustment mid-run cannot make a span appear to end before it started. That is the one piece of shared state the harness needs, and it is deliberately boring. The parent link is implicit in what is open when a span starts, which is exactly the causal structure a trace is supposed to capture. A general-purpose tracer solves the same problem with context propagation (OpenTelemetry uses async-local storage in Node), but this harness only nests two levels deep, and two kinds of span are enough.

## Tracing without touching the loop

The pattern from the last two posts pays off again here. In [post seven](https://raskell.io/articles/the-model-is-a-dependency/) the model became an interface, and in [post eight](https://raskell.io/articles/the-bill-is-part-of-the-loop/) `metered` and `withBudget` wrapped that interface without the loop noticing. Tracing is one more decorator on the same interface.

```typescript
export function traced(inner: Model, tracer: Tracer): Model {
  return {
    name: `traced(${inner.name})`,
    async complete(req) {
      const span = tracer.start("model.complete", "model", { "request.hard": req.hard });
      let error: string | undefined;
      try {
        const res = await inner.complete(req);
        span.attributes["response.model"] = res.model;
        span.attributes["usage.input_tokens"] = res.usage.input_tokens;
        span.attributes["usage.output_tokens"] = res.usage.output_tokens;
        span.attributes["cost.usd"] = costOf(res.model, res.usage);
        return res;
      } catch (err) {
        error = String(err);
        throw err;
      } finally {
        tracer.end(span, error);
      }
    },
  };
}
```

Two attributes on that span do more than they look. `request.hard` is what the loop asked for, a strong model or a cheap one; `response.model` is what actually answered. When the budget from post eight downgrades a hard turn past its soft cap, those two disagree, and the trace records the downgrade as data instead of a mystery. The cost attribute reuses `costOf` from post eight, so the same number the ledger sums is now pinned to the exact span that spent it. (The real file also records the cache read and write counts, which matter more than they look, as the next section shows.)

The tool side is the same move, applied at the one place the loop dispatches tools. It is shorter than the model side, because since post three the registry never throws. A failed tool comes back as a result with `ok: false`, so the wrapper only has to read it.

```typescript
export async function tracedDispatch(
  registry: Registry,
  tracer: Tracer,
  name: string,
  input: Record<string, unknown>,
): Promise<ToolResult> {
  const span = tracer.start(`tool.${name}`, "tool", { "tool.name": name });
  const result = await registry.dispatch(name, input);
  if (result.ok) span.attributes["result.bytes"] = Buffer.byteLength(result.value, "utf8");
  tracer.end(span, result.ok ? undefined : result.error);
  return result;
}
```

The composition order matters, the same way it did for the meter and the budget. The tracer sits outermost, wrapping the whole model chain, because a span should capture what actually happened including the fallback and the downgrade, not the intent before either. The loop itself changes in two places: it opens a span for the run, and a span for each turn, closed in a `finally` so that a turn which ends early still closes. Everything else is a wrapper the loop never sees.

## Reading the shape of a run

This is the part the ledger could not give you. A single run, rendered as its span tree, with duration, tokens, and cost on each node:

```
agent.session                                               5.91s   $0.071
├─ turn 1  easy                                             0.89s   $0.013
│  ├─ model.complete  claude-haiku-4-5  10.3k tok           0.84s   $0.013
│  └─ tool.fs_read  ok                                      0.04s
├─ turn 2  easy                                             2.03s   $0.003
│  ├─ model.complete  claude-haiku-4-5  11.2k tok           0.71s   $0.003
│  ├─ tool.shell  ERROR                                     1.31s
│  └─ tool.fs_read  ok                                      0.04s
├─ turn 3  hard                                             2.34s   $0.050
│  ├─ model.complete  claude-sonnet-4-6  12.1k tok          1.12s   $0.050
│  └─ tool.shell  ok                                        1.22s
└─ turn 4  easy                                             0.66s   $0.005
   └─ model.complete  claude-haiku-4-5  12.5k tok           0.66s   $0.005
```

Read it top to bottom and the run explains itself. Turns one and two ran on Haiku. In turn two the model asked for two tools at once, and they ran side by side: the file read was done in forty milliseconds while the shell command took over a second and failed. Because a tool failed, the loop marked turn three as hard, the router sent it to Sonnet, and Sonnet fixed the command. Turn four went back to Haiku and finished.

That one Sonnet span is seventy percent of the bill, and the reason is not what you would guess. Sonnet's answer was not the expensive part. The cache was. Prompt caches are kept per model, so the first time the router sends a turn to Sonnet, Sonnet has to write its own copy of the ten-thousand-token prefix that Haiku had already cached, and at Sonnet's cache-write price that is nearly four of the five cents. The ledger told you the run cost seven cents. The trace tells you that most of it was one escalation, that most of the escalation was a cache write, and therefore where to look: if escalation is common, the boundary between the tiers is what you are paying for.

No prior post could show you that picture, because each one owned a fragment of it. Routing lived in [post seven](https://raskell.io/articles/the-model-is-a-dependency/), cost in [post eight](https://raskell.io/articles/the-bill-is-part-of-the-loop/), the shell tool in [post two](https://raskell.io/articles/your-agent-wants-root/), the tool registry in [post three](https://raskell.io/articles/tools-how-agents-actually-do-things/). The trace is the first artifact that holds all of them in one frame, because it records the run rather than any one subsystem's view of it.

## When the homegrown tracer stops being enough

The tracer above is about a hundred and fifty lines, including the renderer that prints the tree, and it will carry you a long way. It stops carrying you at the point where you want to keep traces across runs, query them by attribute, compare today's latency against last week's, or hand a trace to someone who is not sitting at your terminal. Building a storage layer, a query language, and a waterfall UI is not a side quest. It is a product, and it already exists several times over.

That is where OpenTelemetry earns the dependency. The upgrade is the same tool-boundary trick the series keeps using: the wrappers only ever call `start` and `end`, so you swap the body of the `Tracer` for an OTel tracer, keep the wrappers, and the loop still never notices. What you get in return is an exporter to any backend that speaks OTLP, Jaeger and Tempo and Honeycomb among them, and a schema other people already understand.

The schema part is worth a beat, because OpenTelemetry has been standardizing exactly this problem. The GenAI semantic conventions define attribute names for model spans so that a trace from your harness and a trace from someone else's mean the same thing:

```typescript
span.setAttributes({
  "gen_ai.operation.name": "chat",
  "gen_ai.response.model": res.model,
  "gen_ai.usage.input_tokens": res.usage.input_tokens,
  "gen_ai.usage.output_tokens": res.usage.output_tokens,
});
```

There is also a `gen_ai.request.model` attribute, and it shows where the conventions assume a simpler world than this harness. The loop never asks for a model by name; it asks for a tier, and the router picks the model. At the layer where `traced` sits there is no requested model id to record, only `request.hard`, which no convention has a name for. That attribute stays a custom one.

Adopt those names on the homegrown span from the start, even before you take the dependency, and the eventual migration is a rename instead of a rewrite. One caveat worth stating plainly: as of mid-2026 the GenAI conventions are still marked experimental and the attribute names have moved between releases. Pin the version you target and expect to touch the mapping again. This is an area where I would keep the indirection of my own attribute names and translate at the export boundary, rather than scatter `gen_ai.*` strings through the harness.

## What not to put on a span

The tempting move, the first time you have spans, is to attach everything. The full prompt, the full completion, every tool result verbatim. Do not, and the reasons are the operational ones that bite later rather than in the demo.

The first is data. Prompts and completions are the most sensitive payload the agent touches. They carry user input, retrieved documents, secrets the model was handed, and whatever the tools read off disk. A span attribute is a copy of that data, shipped to a telemetry backend, retained on its schedule, visible to anyone with query access. A trace store is not the place you want a second uncontrolled copy of every prompt to live. Redact at the boundary, or record a hash and a length instead of the text, and put the full content behind a separate, access-controlled path if you need it at all.

The second is cardinality and cost. Tracing everything at full fidelity is not free, and the bill has the same shape as the token bill from last post: it arrives later and larger than you expected. High-cardinality attributes, unique ids and full text, are what make trace storage expensive and trace queries slow. Sampling is the usual answer, and it has a trap the agent case makes worse. Head sampling, deciding at the start of a run whether to keep it, will throw away the rare expensive trace precisely because it looked ordinary at turn one. If you sample, sample at the tail, after the run's cost and outcome are known, so the forty-cent escalation and the failed tool call are the ones you keep.

A short list of failure modes worth naming, because each one has cost me time somewhere:

- Spans that never close, because an error path skipped the `end` call. The `finally` block above exists for exactly this. An unclosed span silently swallows its children in the tree.
- Clock skew from wall-time timestamps. Use a monotonic clock for durations.
- Attribute explosion, where a well-meaning `attributes["prompt"] = prompt` turns every trace into a storage line item.
- Sampling that hides the incident, covered above.
- A trace that looks complete but is missing the tool subtree, because a tool was called through a path that did not open a span. Coverage of the instrumentation is itself a thing to check.

## Tradeoffs and what this does not solve

The honest edges, as a table, because "it depends" owes you the specifics:

| Concern | Where it holds | Where it breaks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Span tree | Exact causal shape of one run, read top to bottom | Overhead and storage grow with how much you instrument |
| Homegrown tracer | No dependency, readable, ships in one file | No persistence, no query, no UI past the terminal |
| OTel + GenAI semconv | Portable, backend-agnostic, others understand it | Conventions still experimental, names drift between releases |
| Prompt and output on spans | Full fidelity when you are debugging a bad answer | A second uncontrolled copy of sensitive data, plus cost |
| Sampling | Bounds the telemetry bill | Head sampling drops the rare trace you most wanted |

The row to watch is the last content row. A trace is only as safe as the most sensitive thing you put on it, and the pressure to attach the full prompt is strongest at exactly the moment you are debugging something important. Decide the redaction rule once, at the export boundary, and do not relax it per incident.

What this does not solve is judgment. The trace shows you that turn five cost thirty-nine cents and escalated to `opus`. It does not tell you whether that was the right call or a router that panics on hard prompts. It shows you the shell tool failed and retried. It does not tell you whether the migration was safe to retry at all. The trace is the evidence. Reading it is still the job, and knowing whether the run was actually *good*, not just observable, is a different feedback loop and the next post.

## Where this lands in the platform

The loop can now route a turn, fail over when a provider is down, stay inside a budget, and reconstruct exactly what it did when you ask. Four of the properties an agent exposes at runtime, which model answered, whether it was up, what it cost, and the causal shape of the work, are now things the harness reads and records rather than things that happen to it and vanish.

What the harness still cannot do is tell you whether any of it was correct. The trace of a run that produced a wrong answer looks exactly like the trace of a run that produced a right one. Same spans, same tokens, same cost, and the only difference is a judgment nothing in the harness has made yet. Closing that gap, turning outcomes into a signal the loop can be measured against, is where this goes next.

As with every part of the series, the code is in the [companion repository](https://github.com/raskell-io/the-agent-platform-handbook). Each post leaves the agent in a working state, saved as a git tag, so you can check out [`post-09`](https://github.com/raskell-io/the-agent-platform-handbook/tree/post-09) and run the agent exactly as this post leaves it. The change from post eight is small. One new file, `span.ts`, holds the span type and the tracer. A wrapper records every model call, tool calls get the same treatment where they are dispatched, and the loop opens a span for the run and one for each turn.

---
title: "This Site Is Becoming a Map"
url: https://raskell.io/articles/this-site-is-becoming-a-map/
author: Raffael Schneider
date: 2026-10-15
description: "A blog shows what I wrote last. The new map on raskell.io shows what I keep coming back to, and it is the start of a public second brain."
tags: [meta, knowledge-management, hypertext, open-web, zola, external-memory]
---

# This Site Is Becoming a Map

## In short

A blog is a timeline that works for news and badly for ideas, so raskell.io now has a map that draws articles, topics, series and projects as one graph. Every edge comes from a deliberate act, a tag, a series, a link or a named project, and is computed at build time, which avoids the meaningless hairball of similarity-based graph views. The map already showed me two centres of gravity, platform automation and AI engineering, how much *Zentinel* holds together, an isolated corner of older Linux and BSD posts, and projects I never wrote about. It is the first piece of a public second brain: short notes beside long articles, notes that grow, the sources that shaped me, a path from private *Kurumi* notes, and a garden agents can read. The map can be exported as an image or as JSON, and a missing link between two pieces is usually a post I should write.

A blog is a timeline. The newest post sits on top, everything else slides down, and after a while the only way to find the post from last spring is to remember roughly when you read it. That works for news. It works badly for ideas, because ideas do not arrive in date order. Two posts written months apart can be circling the same problem, and nothing on a timeline tells you that.

This site now has a second way in. The [map](https://raskell.io/map/) draws everything here as one graph: every article, every topic, every series, and every project, with a line wherever two of them are actually connected. It is the first piece of something I have wanted for a long time, and this post is about what it is, what it already showed me, and where I want to take it.

## What is on the map

Right now the map holds 32 articles, 20 topics, 2 series, and 21 projects, joined by 266 connections. Pearl dots are articles, cyan dots are topics, champagne dots are series, and rings are projects, grouped under the same headings as the [projects](https://raskell.io/projects/) and [apps](https://raskell.io/apps/) pages. Click a dot and its neighbors light up, along with a short card that tells you what it is and lets you open it.

The connections are the part that matters, so it is worth being precise about where they come from. An article connects to:

- the topics it is tagged with,
- the series it belongs to,
- every other article it links to in its text,
- every project it links to or names.

Projects also connect to the topics they are about, so the things I build sit next to the things I write about, even where I have not written about them yet.

None of this is maintained by hand. The graph is computed when the site is built, in the same template that renders the page. The article-to-article edges are my favorite part, because they come for free from writing:

```jinja
{%- for a in sec.pages %}{% for b in sec.pages %}
  {%- if a.path != b.path and a.content is containing(b.path) %}
    ["a:{{ a.path | safe }}","a:{{ b.path | safe }}"],
  {%- endif %}
{%- endfor %}{% endfor %}
```

If one post links to another, the template finds the other post's path in the rendered body and emits an edge. Every time I cross-reference something, the map grows a line. That is a quiet incentive to cross-reference more, which is exactly the habit I want.

## Why not just tags

The obvious objection is that tags already do this. Every article here has had tags for years, and every tag has a page that lists its articles.

Tags answer one question at a time. The tag page for `platform-automation` tells you what is filed under platform automation. It does not tell you that half of those posts also sit under `ai-engineering`, that many of them link to each other, or that one project ties a cluster of them together. A list per tag is a set of drawers. The map shows you how the drawers overlap.

The second objection is the better one. Anyone who has used Obsidian knows the graph view: a beautiful hairball that looks profound and tells you nothing. A graph is only as good as its edges, and edges drawn from shared words or vague similarity produce exactly that hairball. This is why every edge on the map comes from a deliberate act. I tagged it, I put it in a series, I linked it, or I named the project. If the map looks like a hairball someday, that will be an honest picture of my writing.

## What it already showed me

I expected the map to be a nicer table of contents. It turned out to be a mirror, and not an entirely flattering one.

**Two centers of gravity.** Most of the graph hangs off two topics, `platform-automation` and `ai-engineering`. That is where most of my writing has gone in the last year, and it is a fair summary of what makes me tick right now: how to run systems well, and what changes when software writes software.

**One project holds a lot together.** [Zentinel](https://zentinelproxy.io) has more connections than any other project: eleven articles led to it before this one. Articles about edge systems, security, Rust, and even about how I work all lead back to it. I knew it mattered to me. I did not know it was the load-bearing beam of the site.

**A quiet corner.** The Linux and BSD posts sit off to one side, connected to each other and barely to anything else. They date from 2022 to 2024, an older version of my interests, and the map makes that visible in a way a date never did.

**Things I build and never write about.** [Manabi](https://manabi.raskell.io), [Paw & Claw](https://pawandclaw.raskell.io), and [Terrarium](https://github.com/raskell-io/terrarium) hung off their topics and their group and nothing else. Until this post, not a single article mentioned them. A timeline hides that kind of gap completely. On the map, it is a dot with a thin line or two, and it is hard to unsee.

## Where this is going

The map is the first visible piece of a longer shift. Over the next few years, I want a garden to grow alongside the articles here: a personal but shared map of what I think about, what I build, and what changed my mind.

None of these ideas are new. Vannevar Bush described the [memex](https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/1945/07/as-we-may-think/303881/) in 1945, a desk that would let a reader tie documents together into trails and follow them later, the way the mind follows associations. Andy Matuschak's [evergreen notes](https://notes.andymatuschak.org/Evergreen_notes) and Maggie Appleton's [history of digital gardens](https://maggieappleton.com/garden-history) describe the modern version: notes that grow and get revised instead of being published once and left to age. What I want to add is a specific practice, built on the tools I already trust: plain files, a static site, open formats, no platform in between.

Concretely, that means a few changes, roughly in this order:

1. **Short notes next to long articles.** The long articles stay. They are where I work an idea through properly, with code, trade-offs, and counterarguments. Next to them, I want short notes: a paragraph or a page on an idea, a paper, or a question I have not answered yet. Notes are cheap to write and easy to link, and some of them will become the starting point for a longer piece. The map will show which article grew out of which notes.
2. **Notes that grow.** Some pages should be revised over time rather than frozen on their publication date. The `updated` field already exists, and I want to use it on purpose.
3. **What shaped me.** The books, papers, talks, and people that keep showing up in my thinking deserve to be dots too, so you can follow an idea back to where it came from.
4. **Private to public.** [Kurumi](https://kurumi.raskell.io), the local-first second brain I am building, already has wikilinks, backlinks, and a graph view of its own. Eventually, I want a path for a note to move from a private graph like that to the public one when it is ready, without copying it by hand.
5. **Readable by agents.** Plain files, explicit links, the graph as JSON, and the site's [llms.txt](https://raskell.io/llms.txt) mean an agent can walk this garden as easily as a person can. I want that to stay true as it grows, so the notes can serve as source material for my own agents, and for anyone else's, when they work on something I have thought about before.

I do not know yet how far this goes, or what it looks like when the map has five hundred dots instead of eighty. That is part of the point. A garden is not designed up front.

## A shared map

A personal map published on the web is still, in one sense, just mine. I want it to be a little more than that. The map has an export button: you can download it as an image, or as JSON with every node and every edge. Take the data, draw it differently, connect it to your own notes, or tell me which links are missing. If you think two pieces belong together and the map does not show it, that is usually a post I should write.

## The rest of the relaunch

It has been quiet here since July. I was away for a good part of that time: in Greece, visiting family and swimming in the Ionian Sea, and then in Hong Kong and Okinawa, where I enjoyed the subtropical weather, sat through two typhoons, and went back to the coral reefs and beaches I wrote about in [Looking back on 2025](https://raskell.io/articles/looking-back-on-2025/). The redesign is what I did when I got back.

The map arrived together with a new design for the whole site, a quieter theme called [seijaku](https://github.com/raskell-io/seijaku), from the Japanese word for stillness. The article index is denser and grouped by year, covers are cut automatically from each post's social banner, the tanuki in the corner blinks, and every old URL still works. Most of it was built in a long session with an AI coding agent, the way I described in [How I Work These Days](https://raskell.io/articles/how-i-work-these-days/).

The map's first version had one memorable bug. A single minus sign turned the repulsion between nodes into attraction, and every dot slid into the middle of the canvas until the whole graph was one bright point. It is the most honest picture of a blog I have seen: everything piled in one place, with no way to tell what connects to what.

A blog tells you what I wrote last. The map shows what I keep coming back to.

---
title: "The Bill Is Part of the Loop"
url: https://raskell.io/articles/the-bill-is-part-of-the-loop/
author: Raffael Schneider
date: 2026-07-18
description: "Every model response already carries its own bill in the usage field, and the loop throws it away. This post reads that field, prices it against a table, and turns cost into a value the loop can see per turn and act on: a metering decorator that needs no loop change, a running ledger, prompt-cache accounting that moves the number the most, and a budget that degrades before it stops. Part eight of The Agent Platform Handbook."
tags: [agents, ai-platforms, economics, observability, metrics, typescript]
series: the-agent-platform-handbook
---

# The Bill Is Part of the Loop

## In short

Every model response already carries an exact usage record of input, output, cache write and cache read tokens, yet the loop reads past it and cost only appears later on an aggregated invoice. Pricing that usage against a small per-model table and metering it through a decorator on the model interface gives a per-turn, per-model ledger without changing the loop itself. The first thing the ledger revealed was not a cheaper model but a stable prompt prefix the agent was paying to resend each turn; caching it moves the bill more than routing does. A budget decorator gives the ledger authority: past a soft threshold it forces the cheap model, and at the hard cap it stops the run with a partial answer instead of a runaway bill. The trade-off is that degrading under a soft cap buys a bounded bill rather than a good outcome, and a task that truly needs the strong model may quietly do worse.

> Part 8 of *The Agent Platform Handbook. From Loop to Platform.* Previous: [The Model Is a Dependency](https://raskell.io/articles/the-model-is-a-dependency/). Next: [Observability Is Not Logging](https://raskell.io/articles/observability-is-not-logging/).

[Post seven](https://raskell.io/articles/the-model-is-a-dependency/) pulled the model out of a hardcoded string and made it a dependency the loop can route and fail over. A `Model` is now an interface: `complete(request)` returns a response, and the loop neither knows nor cares whether a cheap model, a strong model, a router, or a fallback chain produced it. The harness sits at tag [`post-07`](https://github.com/raskell-io/the-agent-platform-handbook/tree/post-07).

That interface has a property we have not spent yet. Every response the model returns carries a `usage` object: input tokens, output tokens, cache reads, cache writes. It arrives on every single turn, exact, for free. And the loop reads past it every time.

You find out what an agent cost the way you find out about a gas leak. From the invoice, at the end of the month, long after the loop that caused it has exited. This post reads the number the loop already has, turns it into dollars, and then does the thing the title promises: feeds the bill back into the loop as an input the loop acts on. It ships as tag [`post-08`](https://github.com/raskell-io/the-agent-platform-handbook/tree/post-08).

## How we started paying attention

Cost control did not start with agents. It started with cloud. The FinOps movement grew up around the same problem one layer down: a bill that arrives monthly, aggregated by account, with no line back to the team or the feature that ran up the number. The fix there was chargeback and showback, attributing spend to the thing that caused it, close enough to the moment it happened that someone could still change their behavior.

Agents inherited the problem and made it worse, because an agent spends money in a tight loop with no human in it. The prompt-caching pricing changes of 2024 and 2025 turned the token bill into something you could cut by an order of magnitude if you structured the prompt correctly, and left it untouched if you did not. Gateway products like OpenRouter and Portkey appeared in part to surface per-call cost that the raw provider dashboards buried.

The through-line is the same each time. The bill is a lagging signal until you move it next to the code that generates it. What follows is that move, for one agent loop.

## The number is already in your hand

Here is the response type the SDK hands back on every call, trimmed to the field that matters:

```typescript
type Usage = {
  input_tokens: number;
  output_tokens: number;
  cache_creation_input_tokens: number | null;
  cache_read_input_tokens: number | null;
};
```

Four buckets, and every one of them is priced differently. This is the whole reason the naive approach (count the tokens, multiply by one number) is wrong. A token you write to the cache and a token you read back from it differ in price by more than ten times.

It is worth being precise about why reading this beats reading a dashboard. The provider console shows you the same tokens, but a day late and aggregated per API key, not per task. That is the FinOps problem again, exactly. The `usage` field is a leading signal you already hold. The dashboard is a lagging report you go and fetch. For a loop that has to decide, mid-run, whether it can afford the next turn, only one of those is any use.

## A price is a table, not a constant

A new file, `price.ts`, holds what a turn costs. It starts by naming the four rates, then lists them per model:

```typescript
import type { Usage } from "@anthropic-ai/sdk/resources/messages";

// All four rates in US dollars per million tokens. A price is data, not logic:
// it drifts, so it lives in one table you edit, next to the ids it describes.
export type Price = {
  input: number;
  output: number;
  cacheWrite: number; // 5-minute write, 1.25x input
  cacheRead: number; //  cache hit,      0.1x input
};

const PRICES: Record<string, Price> = {
  "claude-haiku-4-5": { input: 1, output: 5, cacheWrite: 1.25, cacheRead: 0.1 },
  "claude-sonnet-4-6": { input: 3, output: 15, cacheWrite: 3.75, cacheRead: 0.3 },
};
```

A common objection lands here: prices change, so a hardcoded table is already wrong. That is true and it does not matter as much as it sounds. The `usage` counts are exact, straight from the response. Only the multiplier is a guess, and a multiplier that is wrong by a constant factor still ranks turns correctly, still triggers a budget at roughly the right place, still tells you the strong model costs several times the cheap one. The table is a config value you edit in one place when a vendor moves a number. It is not load-bearing precision.

Turning a `usage` record into a cost is then arithmetic:

```typescript
// Price one response. The buckets are summed separately because a cache read
// costs a tenth of fresh input, and that gap is the whole point of caching.
export function costOf(model: string, usage: Usage): number {
  const p = PRICES[model];
  if (!p) throw new Error(`no price for model ${model}`);
  return (
    (usage.input_tokens * p.input +
      usage.output_tokens * p.output +
      (usage.cache_creation_input_tokens ?? 0) * p.cacheWrite +
      (usage.cache_read_input_tokens ?? 0) * p.cacheRead) /
    1_000_000
  );
}
```

That is the entire pricing layer. It knows nothing about the loop, the router, or the budget. It converts a response into a number.

## Metering is a decorator, not a rewrite

Now the payoff for having made the model a dependency in the last post. Cost accounting is not new plumbing threaded through the loop. It is one more decorator on `Model`, the same shape as the `router` and `withFallback` from post seven.

First, somewhere to accumulate:

```typescript
export type Ledger = {
  turns: number;
  cost: number;
  byModel: Record<string, number>;
};

export function newLedger(): Ledger {
  return { turns: 0, cost: 0, byModel: {} };
}
```

Then the decorator. A `metered` model wraps another model, lets it run, reads the `usage` the response already carried, prices it, and files it in the ledger:

```typescript
import type { Model } from "./model";
import { costOf } from "./price";

export function metered(inner: Model, ledger: Ledger): Model {
  return {
    name: `metered(${inner.name})`,
    async complete(req) {
      const res = await inner.complete(req);
      const cost = costOf(res.model, res.usage);
      ledger.turns += 1;
      ledger.cost += cost;
      ledger.byModel[res.model] = (ledger.byModel[res.model] ?? 0) + cost;
      return res;
    },
  };
}
```

Note `res.model`, not the requested model. The router picks a tier and the fallback chain may override it, but the response reports who actually answered. Metering prices the truth, not the intent.

It slots into `defaultModel` between the router and the concrete models, one line changed:

```typescript
export function defaultModel(ledger: Ledger, capUSD: number): Model {
  const haiku = anthropicModel("claude-haiku-4-5");
  const sonnet = anthropicModel("claude-sonnet-4-6");
  const routed = router(withFallback(haiku, sonnet), withFallback(sonnet, haiku));
  return withBudget(metered(routed, ledger), ledger, capUSD);
}
```

The loop calling `defaultModel` never learns that metering happened. That is the same invisibility `withFallback` has, and it is the point. Because the model is an interface, observability composes onto it without touching control flow.

## Attribute the spend, do not just total it

The ledger keeps a per-model breakdown, `byModel`, and that is not decoration. The previous post argued that a tool-driven loop spends most of its turns on routine digestion, which the cheap model handles, and reserves the strong model for the few hard turns. That was an argument. The ledger turns it into a measurement.

Add one line to the loop and every turn prints what it cost:

```typescript
const before = ledger.cost;
const response = await step(model, registry, messages, system, hard);
const turnCost = ledger.cost - before;
console.error(
  `# turn ${i + 1} ${hard ? "hard" : "easy"} -> ${response.model} ` +
    `$${turnCost.toFixed(4)} (run $${ledger.cost.toFixed(4)})`,
);
```

Run a real task and the shape falls out of the log: a long tail of cheap Haiku turns at a fraction of a cent each, punctuated by a handful of Sonnet turns after a tool error, each worth several of the cheap ones. The routing claim from post seven stops being something I asserted and becomes something the ledger prints. That is the quiet value of metering. It closes the loop on the previous post before it does anything new.

## The cache moves the number more than the model does

Here is the part that surprised me, and it is why this post adds caching rather than assuming it.

Look again at `costOf`. A cache read is priced at a tenth of fresh input. The harness has a large, stable prefix on every single turn: the pinned `.AGENTS/` context, the tool descriptions, the memory block, the system prompt. Post six built all of it. And until now, every turn paid full input price to send that prefix again.

Prompt caching is a prefix match. Mark the stable part with a cache breakpoint and the second turn onward reads it back instead of re-sending it. In `model.ts`, the system prompt was a plain string:

```typescript
system: req.system,
```

Wrapping it in a cached block is the whole change:

```typescript
system: [{ type: "text", text: req.system, cache_control: { type: "ephemeral" } }],
```

Now watch the ledger across two turns of the same run. On turn one, `cache_creation_input_tokens` is large: you pay the 1.25x write premium once to seed the cache. On turn two, that same span comes back as `cache_read_input_tokens` at 0.1x, and `input_tokens` collapses to just the new content of the turn. For an agent whose prefix dwarfs its per-turn additions, which is most agents, this is the single largest line item you can move.

The lesson is the ordering. You could not see this win until you were measuring. The first thing the ledger revealed was not a cheaper model to switch to. It was a prefix you were paying to resend. Metering pointed at the fix before it paid for itself.

## A budget is a ledger with authority

Everything so far is observation. Metering watches, it does not act. The title of this post promises the bill becomes part of the loop, and that requires the ledger to grow teeth.

A budget is one more decorator. It reads the running total the ledger has been keeping and, crucially, it degrades before it stops:

```typescript
export class BudgetExceeded extends Error {
  constructor(readonly spent: number, readonly cap: number) {
    super(`budget exceeded: $${spent.toFixed(4)} of $${cap.toFixed(2)}`);
  }
}

export function withBudget(inner: Model, ledger: Ledger, capUSD: number): Model {
  const soft = capUSD * 0.8;
  return {
    name: `budget(${inner.name})`,
    complete(req) {
      if (ledger.cost >= capUSD) throw new BudgetExceeded(ledger.cost, capUSD);
      const overSoft = ledger.cost >= soft;
      // past the soft line, ride the cheap model regardless of the hard flag
      return inner.complete({ ...req, hard: req.hard && !overSoft });
    },
  };
}
```

Two thresholds, two behaviors. Past eighty percent of the cap, the budget clears the `hard` flag before the turn runs, so the router sends the cheap model even on a turn the loop wanted the strong one for. The agent gets slower and dumber, but it keeps going. At the hard cap, it raises `BudgetExceeded` and refuses the turn outright.

The loop catches that and stops with grace instead of a surprise:

```typescript
const ledger = newLedger();
const model = defaultModel(ledger, 0.5); // fifty-cent ceiling for the run

// inside the loop:
try {
  const response = await step(model, registry, messages, system, hard);
  // ... handle the turn
} catch (err) {
  if (err instanceof BudgetExceeded) {
    console.error(`# ${err.message} -- stopping with a partial answer`);
    return;
  }
  throw err;
}
```

An agent that hits its ceiling now returns what it has, with a log line saying why, instead of billing you for a runaway loop you find out about tomorrow. The composition order matters and is worth reading off `defaultModel`: the budget wraps the meter, which wraps the router. The budget reads the total the meter has been filling, and adjusts the request before the router ever sees it. The bill from the last N turns shapes turn N plus one. That sentence is the literal meaning of the title.

## Tradeoffs and what this does not solve

The honest edges, as a table, because "it depends" owes you one:

| Concern | Where it holds | Where it breaks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Token counts | Exact, from the response | Never estimated, so never the weak point |
| Price table | One file, easy to update | You own keeping it current; a vendor change is silent until you edit it |
| Budget | A backstop against runaway loops | Not a scheduler. It caps total spend, it does not plan the cheapest path to the goal |
| Attribution | Per run, per model | Not yet per user or per tenant. That is a platform concern, and it comes later |
| Degrade-before-stop | Keeps the agent alive near the cap | A task that genuinely needs the strong model will do worse under the soft cap, quietly |

The last row is the one to watch in production. Riding the cheap model past the soft cap trades quality for survival on purpose, and on a hard task that trade can produce a confidently worse answer with no error to flag it. The budget buys you a bounded bill, not a good outcome under pressure. Know which one you are asking for.

## Where this lands in the platform

The loop can now route the turn, fail over when a provider is down, and stay inside a spend ceiling while it does. Cost has moved from a report you read the next day to an input the loop consumes on the current turn. Three of the properties the model exposes (which one, whether it is up, what it costs) are now things the harness reads and acts on, rather than things that happen to it.

What the harness still cannot do is tell you what it did. The ledger knows the run cost forty cents across nine turns, but it cannot show you the shape of those turns: which tool failed, which turn escalated, where the time went. That per-turn record is the raw material for a trace, and turning it into one is the next post.

Everything here ships as tag [`post-08`](https://github.com/raskell-io/the-agent-platform-handbook/tree/post-08), the same as every part in the series: a `price.ts`, a `metered` and a `withBudget` decorator, a ledger, and the one line of caching that moved the number the most.
