---
title: "All beginning is Haskell"
url: https://raskell.io/articles/all-beginning-is-haskell/
author: Raffael Schneider
date: 2023-03-06
updated: 2026-03-09
description: "How Haskell shaped the way I think about building systems, and why I am still building Haskell tooling years after writing my first monad."
tags: [programming-languages, haskell, developer-tooling, compilers, type-systems]
---

# All beginning is Haskell

## In short

Haskell rewired how I think about software, not because it is the best language for every task, but because it teaches programs as compositions of well-typed transformations. Its most valuable lesson for me is that types are design tools: algebraic data types make illegal states unrepresentable, and I use the same pattern in Rust constantly. Monads matter less for being clever than for making effects explicit and composable in the type signature, an idea that shapes how I use Result in Rust. The language is excellent but its tooling has gaps, which is why I am building *hx*, a Haskell toolchain CLI in Rust, and *bhc*, an experimental compiler without a garbage collector. My Rust projects, *Conflux*, *Zentinel* and *Shiioo*, carry Haskell ideas such as merge laws, monoids and folds over events, and I believe really learning Haskell makes you a better engineer in any language.

This site is called raskell.io. That is not an accident.

I started learning Haskell because I liked mathematics and someone told me there was a programming language built on top of it. Not "inspired by" in the loose way that every language claims some mathematical foundation. Actually built on lambda calculus, category theory, and type theory, in a way where the math is not decoration but structure.

What I did not expect was how thoroughly it would rewire the way I think about building software. Not because Haskell is the best language for every task. It is not, and I write far more Rust than Haskell these days. But because Haskell teaches you to think about programs in a way that makes you better at everything else.

## What Haskell actually teaches you

Most introductions to Haskell talk about pure functions, immutability, and monads. They are not wrong, but they miss the point. The point is not any single feature. It is how those features combine into a way of thinking about programs as compositions of well-typed transformations.

In an imperative language, you think about sequences of steps. Do this, then that, then check a condition, then loop. The program is a recipe. In Haskell, you think about transformations. What goes in, what comes out, what shape does the data have at each stage. The program is a pipeline.

This sounds abstract until you see it in practice. Suppose you need to process a list of user records: filter out inactive users, extract their email addresses, and normalize them to lowercase.

In an imperative style, you write a loop with conditions and mutations. In Haskell:

```haskell
activeEmails :: [User] -> [Email]
activeEmails = map (normalize . email) . filter isActive
```

One line. Read it right to left: filter active users, then map over the result, extracting and normalizing emails. The type signature tells you what goes in (`[User]`) and what comes out (`[Email]`). No mutation. No intermediate variables. No place for off-by-one errors or null pointer exceptions.

The type signature is not just documentation. It is a contract enforced by the compiler. If `isActive` expects a `User` and you pass it a `String`, the program will not compile. If `normalize` returns an `Email` but you try to use it as a `String`, the program will not compile. The compiler is your first reviewer, and it is tireless.

## Types as design tools

The deeper lesson is that types are not just error catchers. They are design tools.

When I design a system in Haskell, I start with the types. What are the entities? What are the relationships? What transformations are valid? The type system forces you to be precise about these questions before you write any logic. This precision surfaces design problems early, when they are cheap to fix.

Consider modeling a document that can be in one of several states:

```haskell
data Document
  = Draft { content :: Text, author :: UserId }
  | UnderReview { content :: Text, author :: UserId, reviewer :: UserId }
  | Published { content :: Text, author :: UserId, publishedAt :: UTCTime }
```

This is an algebraic data type. Each variant carries exactly the data that makes sense for that state. A `Draft` has no reviewer. A `Published` document has a timestamp. You cannot accidentally access a reviewer on a draft because the type system will not let you. The invalid state is unrepresentable.

This pattern, making illegal states unrepresentable, is perhaps the most valuable idea I took from Haskell. I use it in Rust constantly. Rust's `enum` with associated data is directly descended from Haskell's algebraic data types, and the same design principle applies: encode your invariants in the type system and let the compiler enforce them.

## The monad is not the point

Every Haskell introduction eventually gets to monads, usually with a metaphor involving burritos or boxes. I will skip the metaphor.

A monad is a pattern for sequencing computations that carry some context. The `IO` monad carries the context of interacting with the outside world. The `Maybe` monad carries the context of possible failure. The `State` monad carries the context of mutable state. The pattern is the same in each case: take a value in a context, apply a function that produces a new value in a context, get back a combined context.

```haskell
lookupUser :: UserId -> IO (Maybe User)
lookupUser uid = do
  conn <- getConnection
  result <- query conn "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?" [uid]
  return (listToMaybe result)
```

The `IO` monad here sequences database operations. The `Maybe` handles the case where no user is found. The types tell you both things at a glance: this function does I/O and might not return a result.

The point of monads is not that they are clever. The point is that they make effects explicit and composable. In most languages, a function can do I/O, throw exceptions, mutate global state, or launch missiles, and you cannot tell from its signature. In Haskell, the type signature tells you exactly what effects a function can have. `Int -> Int` is pure. `Int -> IO Int` does I/O. `Int -> Maybe Int` can fail. The information is right there, enforced by the compiler.

This discipline, making effects explicit, changed how I design APIs even in languages that do not enforce it. When I write a Rust function that returns `Result<T, E>`, I am using the same pattern: making failure explicit in the type rather than hiding it behind an exception. Rust learned this from Haskell, and so did I.

## Why I am still building Haskell tooling

If Haskell taught me so much, why do I mostly write Rust?

The honest answer: Haskell's ecosystem has gaps. The language itself is excellent. GHC is one of the most sophisticated compilers ever built. The type system is unmatched in its expressiveness among production languages. But the surrounding infrastructure, the package management, the build tooling, the deployment story, has not kept pace.

Dependency management in Haskell is fragmented. Cabal and Stack coexist with overlapping but incompatible approaches. Build times are long. Cross-compilation is painful. Setting up a Haskell development environment from scratch still involves more friction than it should in 2026.

This is why hx exists. hx is a Haskell toolchain CLI that I am building in Rust. The choice of implementation language is deliberate. Haskell's tooling problems are partly caused by tooling that is itself written in Haskell, creating bootstrap problems and long compile times for the tools themselves. A Rust binary starts instantly, compiles to a single static executable, and cross-compiles trivially. The tool should not have the same dependencies as the thing it manages.

hx is distributed through [mise](https://raskell.io/articles/mise-ate-my-makefile/) (naturally), as well as through AUR, Homebrew, Scoop, and Chocolatey. The goal is that setting up a Haskell project should be as frictionless as setting up a Rust project: one command to install the toolchain, one command to build.

On the other end of the spectrum, bhc (the Basel Haskell Compiler) is an experiment in taking Haskell in a direction GHC was never designed for: compiling Haskell for low-latency runtimes without a garbage collector. The target is workloads like tensor pipelines and real-time systems where GC pauses are not acceptable. bhc is early and ambitious, but it comes from the same conviction: Haskell's ideas deserve better infrastructure than they currently have.

## The Haskell in my Rust

I write Rust the way Haskell taught me to think.

Rust's ownership model is not the same as Haskell's purity, but it serves a similar purpose: it forces you to think about data flow explicitly. In Haskell, you cannot mutate a value because the language will not let you. In Rust, you can mutate, but the borrow checker forces you to be explicit about who owns the data and who can see it. Both languages make you think before you write.

[Conflux](https://github.com/raskell-io/conflux), my CRDT engine, uses algebraic data types for its merge semantics. Each CRDT field type (LwwRegister, GrowOnlySet, ObservedRemoveSet) is an enum variant with associated data, exactly the pattern I described above. The merge function is associative, commutative, and idempotent. These are mathematical properties that I learned to care about from Haskell, where such properties are often expressed as type class laws.

[Zentinel](https://zentinelproxy.io), the reverse proxy, uses Rust's type system to enforce that WAF decisions are handled in the correct pipeline stage. An `AgentDecision` is either `Allow`, `Block`, or `Modify`, and the proxy's merge logic ensures that a `Block` from any agent cannot be overridden. The pattern is a monoid (decisions combine associatively with `Block` as the absorbing element), though nobody would call it that in the Rust codebase. The concept came from Haskell. The implementation is pure Rust.

Even [Shiioo](https://github.com/raskell-io/shiioo), the agentic orchestrator, uses Haskell-influenced patterns. DAG workflows are compositions of typed transformations. Events are algebraic data types with exhaustive pattern matching. The event-sourcing model treats state as a fold over an event stream. `foldl` in Haskell, `Iterator::fold` in Rust. Same idea, different syntax.

## Why "raskell"

The name is a portmanteau. Raffael plus Haskell. I chose it because Haskell is where my engineering thinking started to take its current shape. Not the first language I learned, but the first one that changed how I think about all the others.

I do not believe you need to write Haskell to benefit from Haskell. But I believe that learning it, really learning it, not just reading about monads but building something real with algebraic data types and type classes and higher-order functions, will make you a better engineer in whatever language you actually use.

All beginning is Haskell. The rest is implementation.

# My OpenBSD journey: Getting it virtualized with libvirt (1)

## In short

After moving from Arch to Void Linux, my long fascination with the BSDs led me to start running OpenBSD, beginning with a virtual machine rather than bare metal. I compare Void and OpenBSD, noting shared traits like open source and security focus, and differences in licence, philosophy, package management and init system. OpenBSD stands out for its security focus under Theo de Raadt and for tools adopted elsewhere, such as OpenSSH, and features like pledge and unveil. The guide shows that libvirt with QEMU is enough to run OpenBSD without VirtualBox or VMware: install the packages, fetch and verify the ISO, define the machine with virt-install, and connect over VNC.

## Void Linux as my daily driver

Around six months ago, I decided to ditch my long in the tooth Arch-based setup on my belovest Thinkpad X1 Carbon. I've been very loyal over the years, and almost came to belive that Arch will be a constant in my adult life. While I kept up with upcoming technologies, I somehow lost track of the ever so diversifying landscape of Linux distributions. It took me a while of constantly coming across a generically named reference to what seemed to be yet another Linux distribution. That outwardly generic sounding name, [Void Linux](https://voidlinux.org/), kept poking my curiosity by supposedly feeling like Arch Linux in the old days, while sharing some substantial DNA with the BSD operating systems. Yet, that's another story I might tell another day, but to remain brief, the BSDs, in particular the infamous OpenBSD with its quite infamous lead developer Theo De Raadt, always were what I considered the endgame. The holy grail of Unix operating systems, so did I think over the decades, FreeBSD, NetBSD and OpenBSD, have always been on my personal radar and I felt I had to earn the intellectual capacity to be able to properly put them at use one day. Last year, when I made the (almost painless) switch from Arch Linux to Void Linux, the simplicity and especially the barebone experience of Void reignited the fascination and the admiration I always had for the BSD operating systems and their philosophy.

While I could write (and definitely will in the near future) about how my journey onto Void Linux and how it has been so far, I preferred to write down, in some like diary, and document every step on how one can approach and ultimately use [OpenBSD](https://www.openbsd.org/) in 2023. Big disclaimer, I've yet to install OpenBSD on some baremetal server I ordered some days ago, but dabbled around in the meantime with OS-level virtualization in order to get it running. That's what brings me to _libvirt_ and my surprise to learn that I wouldn't need some full-fledged virtualization solution like the ones offered by VirtualBox or VMWare to efficiently run a virtualized OpenBSD machine. So, ok, let's recap, so far we got the following bill of materials:

- Void Linux as the host system
- OpenBSD to be virtualized on that host system
- libvirt as the glue that makes virtualization feel like black magic

### From Void to OpenBSD

Before I tell you more about the history of how things went down while setting up OpenBSD, let me give you some basic notions about both Void Linux, being one out of many Linux distributions for the sake of simplicity representing them all as it ended up being my distribution of choice, and OpenBSD. As already mentioned earlier, Void Linux and OpenBSD are both Unix-like operating systems, but they feature enough differences to make them noteworthy. Here are a few similarities and differences between the two:

What is similar:

- Both are free and open-source operating systems.
- Both use a package manager for software management. Void Linux uses XBPS, while OpenBSD uses pkg_add.
- Both prioritize security and stability in their development and design.
- Both feature a version control based package repository, meaning that changes in build definition are managed by pull requests from users.

What is different:

- License: Void Linux is licensed under the MIT License, while OpenBSD is licensed under the ISC License.
- Philosophy: OpenBSD prioritizes security and privacy, while Void Linux prioritizes simplicity and modularity.
- Package Management: Void Linux uses the XBPS binary package manager, while OpenBSD uses pkg_add (also binary). OpenBSD additionally has a ports system for building from source.
- Package Repository: Void Linux has a large and diverse repository, while OpenBSD has a smaller and more curated repository.
- Init System: Void Linux uses runit as its init system, while OpenBSD uses rc. None uses the infamous systemd init system.

## What is OpenBSD in a nutshell

OpenBSD is a free and open-source operating system that focuses on security, standardization, and robustness. It is based on the Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) Unix operating system and is developed by a global community of volunteers. OpenBSD aims to provide a secure platform for both personal and enterprise use by implementing strong security features, including access control mechanisms, encryption, and auditing.

[Theo de Raadt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theo_de_Raadt) is the founder and lead developer of OpenBSD. His main objective with OpenBSD is to create a secure operating system that is free from backdoors, vulnerabilities, and other security weaknesses. He is committed to auditing the source code of the operating system and third-party software included with it, to identify and remove any potential security risks. De Raadt is also dedicated to improving the overall quality of the codebase and ensuring compatibility with a wide range of hardware and software. 

What makes OpenBSD really special and stand out is that is developed a suite of tools that got adopted by other OSs like Linux, macOS or even Windows. One of the most famous instances of such adoption is the now de facto standard openssh suite. It actually emerged from within the development circle of the OpenBSD project. OpenBSD also implemented a wide range of OS features that are by now considered staples among other OSs, things like Linux-based OS-level containerization done via the means of cgroups, something that OpenBSD already pioneered and solved with a different spin many years before Linux with pledge and unveil. Go check out [Why OpenBSD rocks](https://why-openbsd.rocks/fact/freezero/) to get a feel what makes OpenBSD so unique and interesting.

### Virtualization with libvirt

So now, let's get back to our virtualization endeavour where we would like to virtualize OpenBSD on a Void Linux installation. If you happen to be using another Linux distribution, most of the individual steps would be very similar. That brings me to the next technology we should explain a bit more here, and that is libvirt.

[libvirt](https://libvirt.org/) is an open-source virtualization management library that provides a simple and unified API for managing virtualization technologies, including KVM, QEMU, Xen, and others. It aims to simplify the process of creating, managing, and migrating virtual machines, storage, and networks, and to make it easier for administrators to manage virtual environments.

To virtualize an operating system like OpenBSD with libvirt, you need to follow these steps:

1. Install libvirt and the virtualization technology you want to use, such as KVM.
2. Download the OpenBSD iso file and place it in a location accessible by libvirt.
3. Create a new virtual machine in libvirt with the OpenBSD ISO as the installation media. This can be done through the command line or using a graphical user interface such as virt-manager.
4. Configure the virtual machine, including the amount of memory, CPU, and disk space, to meet the requirements of OpenBSD.
5. Start the virtual machine and install OpenBSD as you would on a physical machine.
6. Once the installation is complete, you can configure the virtual network, storage, and other settings as required.
7. Finally, you can use the libvirt API or the command line to manage and control the virtual machine, including starting, stopping, migrating, and snapshotting.

### Step-by-step guide

Let's first install the `libvirt` package and some related packages which we need in order to connect via VNC. The VNC will provide us with the possibility to use the graphical interface of the running OpenBSD instance.

```bash
$ sudo xbps-install -S dbus qemu libvirt virt-manager virt-viewer tigervnc
```

Now, we need to add our user, in my case `raskell`, to the `libvirt` group which got simultanously created with the installation of libvirt.

```bash
$ sudo usermod -aG libvirt raskell
```

OpenBSD features a release cycle of six months. We would need to update our system every six month to keep up with the latest packages. During a given release, only security and bug fix patches are applied to the curated packages maintained by pkg_add. Therefore, in February 2023, we're using the [OpenBSD 7.2](https://www.openbsd.org/72.html) release version. As I'm living in Switzerland, I chose to pull the iso image from a Swiss mirror, in this case from [`mirror.ungleich.ch/pub/OpenBSD`](https://mirror.ungleich.ch/pub/OpenBSD/7.2/) (check what mirror is closest to you to get the best download rate).

```bash
# cd /var/lib/libvirt/boot/
# sudo wget https://mirror.ungleich.ch/pub/OpenBSD/7.2/amd64/install72.iso
--2023-01-12 20:48:15--  https://mirror.ungleich.ch/pub/OpenBSD/7.2/amd64/install72.iso

Connecting to mirror.ungleich.ch (mirror.ungleich.ch)|2a0a:e5c0:2:2:400:c8ff:fe68:bef3|:443... connected.

sudo wget https://mirror.ungleich.ch/pub/OpenBSD/7.2/amd64/SHA256
--2023-01-12 20:47:38--  https://mirror.ungleich.ch/pub/OpenBSD/7.2/amd64/SHA256
Resolving mirror.ungleich.ch (mirror.ungleich.ch)... 2a0a:e5c0:2:2:400:c8ff:fe68:bef3, 185.203.114.135
Connecting to mirror.ungleich.ch (mirror.ungleich.ch)|2a0a:e5c0:2:2:400:c8ff:fe68:bef3|:443... connected.

# grep install63.iso SHA256 > /tmp/x
# sha256sum -c /tmp/x
# rm /tmp/x
```

Before we can start the virtualization server and get running our OpenBSD instance, we need to define the configuraiton on how to virtualize and ultimately boot the system with. This is done with `virt-install`. Noteworthy here is that we [QEMU](https://www.qemu.org/) as our emulation solution of choice, we allocate up to 4GB of RAM and 4 CPU cores to the machine.

```bash
$ sudo virt-install \
      --name=openbsd \
      --virt-type=qemu \
      --memory=2048,maxmemory=4096 \
      --vcpus=2,maxvcpus=4 \
      --cpu host \
      --os-variant=openbsd7.0 \
      --cdrom=/var/lib/libvirt/boot/install72.iso \
      --network=bridge=virbr0,model=virtio \
      --graphics=vnc \
      --disk path=/var/lib/libvirt/images/openbsd.qcow2,size=40,bus=virtio,format=qcow2
```

Once, it is up and running, we can use a vnc solution to connect to the running machine. In this case, I chose [virsh](https://www.libvirt.org/manpages/virsh.html) to do the job. virsh is a command-line interface tool for managing virtualization environments created with libvirt. It allows us to manage virtual machines, storage pools, and network interfaces, as well as other virtualization components, from the command line.

To establish a VNC connection with a running libvirt virtualized OpenBSD instance, you can use the following steps:

1. Start the virtual machine in libvirt: You can start the virtual machine using the virsh command **`virsh start <vm-name>`**, where **`<vm-name>`** is the name of the virtual machine you want to start.
2. Find the VNC display: Once the virtual machine is running, you can find the VNC display number for the virtual machine using the virsh command **`virsh vncdisplay <vm-name>`**.
3. Connect to the VNC display: You can connect to the VNC display using a VNC client, such as **`vncviewer`**, and specify the IP address of the host running the virtual machine and the VNC display number. For example, if the host's IP address is **`192.168.0.100`** and the VNC display number is **`:0`**, the command to connect would be **`vncviewer 192.168.0.100:0`**.
4. Authenticate to the VNC server: You may need to enter a password to authenticate to the VNC server. The password is set when the virtual machine is created in libvirt.

With these steps, you can establish a VNC connection with a running libvirt virtualized OpenBSD instance and interact with the virtual machine's graphical user interface.

```bash
$ virsh dumpxml openbsd | grep vnc
<graphics type='vnc' port='5900' autoport='yes' listen='127.0.0.1'>
```

Like I did, most of you would like to interact with a graphical interface such as with X11. For that, we yet another tool, a so-called VNC viewer. A very simple implementation of such a vnc viewer is [tigervnc](https://tigervnc.org/) (simply install it with `$ sudo xbps-install -S tigervnc`).

```bash
$ sudo virsh --connect
qemu:///system start openbsd
Domain 'openbsd' started
```

# Hello and outlook

## In short

This first post introduces raskell.io as a place to document real work and share patterns other engineers can use, not thought leadership or personal branding. The original plan was to write about Linux and BSD systems such as Void and OpenBSD, open-source tooling, platform automation and whatever hard problem I was stuck on. Looking back from 2026, the scope grew to include edge systems and AI-assisted engineering, held together by one thread: systems under pressure and the tools that keep them running.

## Hello world

This is the first post on raskell.io. My name is Raffael. I build software, mostly in the space of platform automation, edge infrastructure, and applied security. I also have a long-running interest in open-source software, operating systems, and the kind of hardware you find in recycling bins and give a second life to.

This site exists to document real work and share patterns that other engineers can use. Not thought leadership. Not personal branding. Just notes from the workshop.

## What to expect

At the time of writing, I planned to cover:

- Linux and BSD systems, particularly [Void Linux](https://voidlinux.org/) and [OpenBSD](https://www.openbsd.org/)
- Open-source tooling and infrastructure
- Platform automation and operability
- Whatever hard problem I happened to be stuck on

Looking back from 2026, the scope grew to include edge systems, AI-assisted engineering, and a few deep dives I did not expect to write. The thread that held it together was always the same: systems under pressure, and the tools that keep them running.

## References

- [Void Linux](https://voidlinux.org/)
- [OpenBSD](https://www.openbsd.org/)
- [raskell.io source](https://github.com/raskell-io/www.raskell.io)

- *Artificial Intelligence*: A Guide for Thinking Humans by Melanie Mitchell (book, 2019). What AI can and cannot do, from vision to language, by a researcher who studies analogy and abstraction
- *Deep Thinking*: Where Machine Intelligence Ends and Human Creativity Begins by Garry Kasparov (book, 2017). Kasparov on his matches against Deep Blue and what machine intelligence means for human creativity
- *Understanding Deep Learning* by Simon J. D. Prince (book, 2023). A modern textbook on deep learning, from the basics through transformers, diffusion models, and reinforcement learning
- *Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch)* by Sebastian Raschka (book, 2024). Building a GPT-style language model step by step in PyTorch, from tokens and attention to pretraining and fine-tuning
- *AI Engineering*: Building Applications with Foundation Models by Chip Huyen (book, 2025). Building applications on foundation models: evaluation, prompting, retrieval, agents, fine-tuning, and serving
- *Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction* by Richard S. Sutton and Andrew G. Barto (book, 2018). The standard text on reinforcement learning: bandits, dynamic programming, temporal difference learning, and policy gradients
- *Probabilistic Machine Learning: An Introduction* by Kevin P. Murphy (book, 2022). Machine learning from a probabilistic point of view, the first of Murphy's two volumes
- *The Making of the Atomic Bomb* by Richard Rhodes (book, 1986). The history of the atomic bomb from the physics of the atom to Hiroshima, and the scientists who built it
- *Seeing Like a State*: How Certain Schemes to Improve the Human Condition Have Failed by James C. Scott (book, 1998). Why grand state plans fail when they make the world legible and simple, and ignore local, practical knowledge
- *A Peace to End All Peace*: The Fall of the Ottoman Empire and the Creation of the Modern Middle East by David Fromkin (book, 1989). How the Allies broke up the Ottoman Empire after the First World War and drew the borders of the modern Middle East
- *The Billion-Dollar Molecule*: The Quest for the Perfect Drug by Barry Werth (book, 1994). Inside Vertex Pharmaceuticals in its early years, as it tried to design drugs from the structure of proteins
- *The Eighth Day of Creation*: The Makers of the Revolution in Biology by Horace Freeland Judson (book, 1979). The founding of molecular biology, from the structure of DNA to the genetic code, from the scientists themselves
- *The Demon Under the Microscope*: From Battlefield Hospitals to Nazi Labs, One Doctor's Heroic Search for the World's First Miracle Drug by Thomas Hager (book, 2006). Gerhard Domagk and the discovery of the sulfa drugs, the first medicines that beat bacterial infection
- *The Butchering Art*: Joseph Lister's Quest to Transform the Grisly World of Victorian Medicine by Lindsey Fitzharris (book, 2017). Joseph Lister and the fight to make surgery safe through antisepsis, in the hospitals of Victorian Britain
- *Deep Dive*: Exploring the Real-world Value of Open Source Intelligence by Rae L. Baker (book, 2023). Methods and tools for open source intelligence: finding, checking, and connecting what people and organisations leave online
- *Palo Alto*: A History of California, Capitalism, and the World by Malcolm Harris (book, 2023). The history of Silicon Valley as a history of capitalism, from railroads and eugenics to the tech industry
- *Strategy*: A History by Lawrence Freedman (book, 2013). Strategy from the Bible and the Greeks to military, revolutionary, and business strategy today
- *The Lost Art of Scripture*: Rescuing the Sacred Texts by Karen Armstrong (book, 2019). How sacred texts were once read as practice and ritual rather than as literal truth, across the world's religions
- *If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies*: Why Superhuman AI Would Kill Us All by Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares (book, 2025). The case that superhuman AI built with current methods would end humanity, and why the authors want it stopped
- *The Scaling Era*: An Oral History of AI, 2019–2025 by Dwarkesh Patel, with Gavin Leech (book, 2025). An oral history of the years when scaling models became the path to AI, in the words of the people building them
- *Situational Awareness*: The Decade Ahead by Leopold Aschenbrenner (essay, 2024). An essay series arguing that AGI may arrive by 2027 and set off a national-security race for superintelligence
- *The Thinking Machine*: Jensen Huang, Nvidia, and the World's Most Coveted Microchip by Stephen Witt (book, 2025). Jensen Huang and how Nvidia bet the company on the chips that made modern AI possible
- *A Brief History of Intelligence*: Evolution, AI, and the Five Breakthroughs That Made Our Brains by Max Bennett (book, 2023). Five breakthroughs in the evolution of the brain, each paired with the AI technique that echoes it
- *These Strange New Minds*: How AI Learned to Talk and What It Means by Christopher Summerfield (book, 2025). How large language models learned to talk, and what they are and are not, by a neuroscientist who has worked at DeepMind
- *AI Snake Oil*: What Artificial Intelligence Can Do, What It Can't, and How to Tell the Difference by Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor (book, 2024). Which kinds of AI work and which are sold as working, with tools to tell the difference
- *Deep Learning*: Foundations and Concepts by Christopher M. Bishop and Hugh Bishop (book, 2024). A textbook on the core ideas of deep learning, from probability and neural networks to transformers and diffusion
- *Deep Utopia*: Life and Meaning in a Solved World by Nick Bostrom (book, 2024). What people would live for once superintelligence has solved every practical problem
- *Slouching Towards Utopia*: An Economic History of the Twentieth Century by J. Bradford DeLong (book, 2022). The economic history of 1870 to 2010, when humanity first escaped scarcity and still did not reach utopia
- *Abundance* by Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson (book, 2025). Why rich countries fail to build the housing, energy, and infrastructure they can afford, and how to change that
- *Four Futures*: Life After Capitalism by Peter Frase (book, 2016). Four possible futures after capitalism, from abundance or scarcity crossed with equality or hierarchy
- *Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren* by John Maynard Keynes (essay, 1930). Keynes's 1930 prediction that a century of growth would solve the economic problem and leave us with leisure
- *From Counterculture to Cyberculture*: Stewart Brand, the Whole Earth Network, and the Rise of Digital Utopianism by Fred Turner (book, 2006). How Stewart Brand and the Whole Earth network turned the counterculture into Silicon Valley's belief in networks
- *Cybernetic Revolutionaries*: Technology and Politics in Allende's Chile by Eden Medina (book, 2011). Project Cybersyn, the attempt in Allende's Chile to run the economy with cybernetics and a telex network
- *Red Plenty* by Francis Spufford (novel, 2010). A novel about the Soviet dream of planning the economy into abundance with mathematics and computers
- *To Be a Machine*: Adventures Among Cyborgs, Utopians, Hackers, and the Futurists Solving the Modest Problem of Death by Mark O'Connell (book, 2017). A journalist among transhumanists: cryonics, mind uploading, cyborgs, and the people who want to end death
- *The Age of Em*: Work, Love, and Life when Robots Rule the Earth by Robin Hanson (book, 2016). An economist works out what a world run by emulated human brains would look like, in detail
- *More Everything Forever*: AI Overlords, Space Empires, and Silicon Valley's Crusade to Control the Fate of Humanity by Adam Becker (book, 2025). A critique of the futures tech billionaires want: superintelligence, space colonies, and living forever
- *The Player of Games* by Iain M. Banks (novel, 1988). A game player from the Culture, a post-scarcity civilisation, is sent to play for an empire's throne
- *Accelerando* by Charles Stross (novel, 2005). The singularity across three generations of one family, from present-day hackers to post-human minds
- *The Dispossessed*: An Ambiguous Utopia by Ursula K. Le Guin (novel, 1974). Two societies built on opposite answers to property, seen through one physicist who belongs fully to neither
- *Gravity's Rainbow* by Thomas Pynchon (novel, 1973). The V-2 rocket as the centre of a web of war, industry, and paranoia, and the canonical maximalist novel
- *Against the Day* by Thomas Pynchon (novel, 2006). Mathematicians, anarchists, and balloonists in the decades before the First World War, at about 1,100 pages
- *The Recognitions* by William Gaddis (novel, 1955). Forgery, authenticity, and money in the art world, which reads differently now that machines produce convincing copies
- *2666* by Roberto Bolaño (novel, 2004). Five linked books that close in on a city of unsolved murders, and one of the central maximalist novels
- *Cryptonomicon* by Neal Stephenson (novel, 1999). Codebreaking in the Second World War and a data haven in the 1990s, told by someone who enjoys explaining how things work
- *The Name of the Rose* by Umberto Eco (novel, 1980). A murder mystery in a medieval library, about who controls knowledge and what it is allowed to say
- *Das Glasperlenspiel* by Hermann Hesse (novel, 1943). A game that connects every field of knowledge, and the man who masters it and then leaves
- *Solaris* by Stanisław Lem (novel, 1961). An intelligence that resists every attempt at interpretation, and what that failure reveals about the people trying
- *A Canticle for Leibowitz* by Walter M. Miller Jr. (novel, 1959). How knowledge survives a collapse, turns into relics, and returns with the same dangers
- *The Andromeda Strain* by Michael Crichton (novel, 1969). A scientific investigation of an unknown organism, told almost as a case file
- *Airframe* by Michael Crichton (novel, 1996). An incident investigation in a complex system, where the popular explanation arrives before the evidence
- *Gödel, Escher, Bach*: An Eternal Golden Braid by Douglas R. Hofstadter (book, 1979). How meaning and a self can arise from meaningless symbols, through Gödel's incompleteness, Escher's drawings, and Bach's fugues
- *Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs* by Harold Abelson and Gerald Jay Sussman, with Julie Sussman (book, 1985). MIT's introduction to programming through Scheme: abstraction with procedures and data, state, streams, and interpreters and compilers written in the language they interpret
- *Chaos*: Making a New Science by James Gleick (book, 1987). The scientists who found order in turbulence, weather, and dripping taps, and founded the science of chaos
- *Genius*: The Life and Science of Richard Feynman by James Gleick (book, 1992). Richard Feynman's life and physics, from Los Alamos and quantum electrodynamics to the Challenger inquiry
- *Faster*: The Acceleration of Just About Everything by James Gleick (book, 1999). How technology sped up daily life, from the elevator door-close button to the minute-by-minute schedule
- *What Just Happened*: A Chronicle from the Information Frontier by James Gleick (book, 2002). Essays from the years the internet arrived in everyday life, on email, search, spam, and digital identity
- *Isaac Newton* by James Gleick (book, 2003). A short life of Newton built from his own notebooks and letters, from alchemy and theology to the laws of motion
- *The Information*: A History, a Theory, a Flood by James Gleick (book, 2011). Information from talking drums and the telegraph to Shannon's theory, genes as code, and the flood of data today
- *Time Travel*: A History by James Gleick (book, 2016). How time travel became an idea, from H. G. Wells onward, and what it says about how we think of time
- *The Telephone*: A New History by James Gleick (book, 2026). A new history of the telephone and the network it wired around the world; published in November 2026
- *Mathematics and the Unexpected* by Ivar Ekeland (book, 1984). Chaos, catastrophe theory, and chance, from Kepler to Thom, and why the future stays hard to predict; one of the inspirations for Ian Malcolm in Jurassic Park

## Read

- *Ocean*: Earth's Last Wilderness by David Attenborough and Colin Butfield (book, 2025, finished October 2026). Life in the ocean, what it has lost, and how protecting the sea lets it recover
- *The Infinity Machine*: Demis Hassabis, DeepMind, and the Quest for Superintelligence by Sebastian Mallaby (book, 2026, finished October 2026, rated 8.5/10). Demis Hassabis and DeepMind, from game-playing programs and AlphaGo to AlphaFold and the race toward general intelligence. Review: https://raskell.io/articles/win-everything-control-no-one/
- *The Cauldron*: The Making of the Modern Middle East by Simon Sebag Montefiore (book, 2026, finished September 2026). A history of the whole modern Middle East, in all its diversity, from 1900 to the present
- *AI 2040: Plan A* by Thomas Larsen, Romeo Dean, Brendan Halstead, Eli Lifland, Ryan Greenblatt, and Daniel Kokotajlo (report, 2026, finished July 2026). A recommended path rather than a forecast: the United States and China slow down, verify each other, and make a deal
- *From Worm to Human: Scaling Brain Emulation* by Isaak Freeman (paper, 2026, finished June 2026). A thesis that treats brain emulation as an engineering programme, and whose numbers read like a capacity plan
- *State of Brain Emulation Report 2025* by Zanichelli, Schons, Freeman, Shiu, and Arkhipov (report, 2025, finished June 2026). The field's own survey of where connectomics, recording, and modelling stand, and how far apart they still are
- *The Ultimate Hidden Truth of the World*: Essays by David Graeber (book, 2024, finished February 2026). Essays from across Graeber's career on debt, bureaucracy, play, value, and the freedom to make the world differently
- *Guns, Germs, and Steel*: The Fates of Human Societies by Jared Diamond (book, 1997, finished November 2025). Why some societies came to dominate others: geography, crops, animals, and germs rather than any difference in people
- *Nuclear War: A Scenario* by Annie Jacobsen (book, 2024, finished October 2025). A minute-by-minute account of how a nuclear exchange would unfold, built on interviews with the people who plan for one
- *Infinite Jest* by David Foster Wallace (novel, 1996, finished October 2025). A tennis academy, a halfway house, and a film so entertaining it kills, in a near-future North America
- *The Maximalist Novel*: From Thomas Pynchon's Gravity's Rainbow to Roberto Bolaño's 2666 by Stefano Ercolino (book, 2014, finished October 2025). A literary study that defines the maximalist novel as a genre, from Gravity's Rainbow and Infinite Jest to 2666
- *This Is for Everyone*: The Unfinished Story of the World Wide Web by Tim Berners-Lee (book, 2025, finished October 2025, rated 8/10). Read on the shores of Okinawa: the web as a commons, how far what we built drifted from it, and why the models exist at all. Review: https://raskell.io/articles/the-web-was-the-training-set/
- *Pirate Enlightenment, or the Real Libertalia* by David Graeber (book, 2023, finished October 2025). Pirate settlements on Madagascar and the Malagasy experiments in self-government that may have fed the European Enlightenment
- *Jurassic Park* by Michael Crichton (novel, 1990, finished July 2025). A park of cloned dinosaurs, and a mathematician who uses chaos theory to explain why it cannot stay under control
- *Codebreaking*: A Practical Guide by Elonka Dunin and Klaus Schmeh (book, 2020, finished April 2025). A hands-on guide to breaking classical ciphers and codes, with real cases solved and unsolved
- *AI 2027* by Daniel Kokotajlo, Scott Alexander, Thomas Larsen, Eli Lifland, and Romeo Dean (report, 2025, finished April 2025). A month-by-month scenario of AI progress to superintelligence by 2027, with two endings: a race and a slowdown
- *The Island at the Center of the World*: The Epic Story of Dutch Manhattan and the Forgotten Colony That Shaped America by Russell Shorto (book, 2004, finished January 2025). Dutch New Amsterdam, rebuilt from its own archives, and the tolerance and trade it left to Manhattan and America
- *@War*: The Rise of the Military-Internet Complex by Shane Harris (book, 2014, finished September 2024). How the NSA, Cyber Command, and private contractors turned the internet into a domain of war
- *The Books of Jacob* by Olga Tokarczuk (novel, 2014, finished August 2024). Jacob Frank, an eighteenth-century self-proclaimed messiah, and the followers who crossed Europe and three religions with him
- *Future Science*: Essays from the Cutting Edge by Max Brockman (editor) (book, 2011, finished May 2024). Essays by young scientists on the questions at the front of their fields, from neuroscience to physics
- *Crafting Interpreters* by Robert Nystrom (book, 2021, finished 2024). Two complete interpreters for one small language, a tree-walker in Java and a bytecode virtual machine in C
- *Science After Babel* by David Berlinski (book, 2023, finished 2023). Essays that question how much modern science can actually explain, from physics and cosmology to Darwinian biology
- *Network Programming with Go*: Code Secure and Reliable Network Services from Scratch by Adam Woodbeck (book, 2021, finished 2023). Network services in Go from the socket up: TCP, UDP, HTTP, TLS, and keeping them secure and observable
- *Elixir in Action* by Saša Jurić (book, 2019, finished 2023). Elixir and the BEAM for building concurrent, fault-tolerant systems with processes, supervisors, and OTP
- *Wer regiert das Geld?*: Banken, Demokratie und Täuschung by Paul Schreyer (book, 2016, finished 2023). Who may create money and who decides how it is used, read as a question of power and democracy
- *Programming Rust*: Fast, Safe Systems Development by Jim Blandy, Jason Orendorff, and Leonora F. S. Tindall (book, 2021, finished 2023). Rust for systems programmers: ownership, borrowing, traits, concurrency, and unsafe code, explained in depth
- *Site Reliability Engineering*: How Google Runs Production Systems by Betsy Beyer, Chris Jones, Jennifer Petoff, and Niall Richard Murphy (book, 2016, finished 2023). How Google runs production: error budgets, service level objectives, toil, on-call, and postmortems
- *Who We Are and How We Got Here*: Ancient DNA and the New Science of the Human Past by David Reich (book, 2018, finished 2023). What ancient DNA reveals about human prehistory: migrations, mixtures, and populations that no longer exist
- *Building a Second Brain*: A Proven Method to Organize Your Digital Life and Unlock Your Creative Potential by Tiago Forte (book, 2022, finished 2022). A method for keeping notes outside your head: capture, organise, distil, and express, with the PARA folders
- *Rust Web Programming* by Maxwell Flitton (book, 2021, finished 2022). Building web applications and services in Rust, from routing and databases to authentication and deployment
- *Skin in the Game*: Hidden Asymmetries in Daily Life by Nassim Nicholas Taleb (book, 2018, finished 2022). Why whoever takes risks for others should carry the consequences, from Hammurabi's builders to bankers and insurers
- *The Phoenix Project*: A Novel about IT, DevOps, and Helping Your Business Win by Gene Kim, Kevin Behr, and George Spafford (novel, 2013, finished 2022). A novel about an IT manager saving a failing project, and the DevOps ideas he learns along the way
- *Foucault's Pendulum* by Umberto Eco (novel, 1988, finished January 2021). Three Milan editors invent a secret history of the world as a game, and others begin to take it seriously
- *Programming WebAssembly with Rust* by Kevin Hoffman (book, 2019, finished 2021). WebAssembly from the raw text format up to Rust modules that run in the browser and beyond it
- *WebAssembly: The Definitive Guide* by Brian Sletten (book, 2021, finished 2021). What WebAssembly is and how to use it from many languages, in the browser, on servers, and through WASI
- *Der Kampf um die Deutung der Neuzeit*: Die geschichtsphilosophische Diskussion in Deutschland vom Ersten Weltkrieg bis zum Mauerfall by Hauke Ritz (book, 2014, finished November 2020). The German debate in the philosophy of history from the First World War to 1989 about how to understand the modern age
- *Das Tagebuch der Menschheit*: Was die Bibel über unsere Evolution verrät by Carel van Schaik and Kai Michel (book, 2016, finished August 2020). The Bible read as a record of how people coped with settled life, property, and disease, seen through evolution
- *Debt*: The First 5,000 Years by David Graeber (book, 2011, finished 2019). Credit came before coins: five thousand years of debt, and why money was a record of trust long before it was metal
- *The Art of War* by Sun Tzu (book, finished June 2018). An ancient Chinese treatise on strategy: deception, terrain, knowing yourself and the enemy, and winning without fighting
- *These Truths*: A History of the United States by Jill Lepore (book, 2018, finished 2018). The history of the United States as a test of the truths in its founding documents: equality, sovereignty, and consent
- *The Black Swan*: The Impact of the Highly Improbable by Nassim Nicholas Taleb (book, 2007, finished 2018). Rare, high-impact events that nobody predicted and everybody explains afterwards, and why models break exactly where it matters
- *Jerusalem: The Biography* by Simon Sebag Montefiore (book, 2011, finished 2017). Three thousand years of Jerusalem through the empires, faiths, and families that fought over it
- *Freeland*: A Social Anticipation by Theodor Hertzka (novel, 1890, finished 2017). A utopian novel about a colony in East Africa built on free land and free access to capital
- *Das soziale Problem* by Theodor Hertzka (book, 1912, finished 2017). Hertzka on the social question, the problem his novel Freeland set out to answer
- *Language*: The Cultural Tool by Daniel Everett (book, 2012, finished January 2016). Language as a cultural invention rather than an innate grammar, argued from the Pirahã of the Amazon
- *The Devil's Delusion*: Atheism and Its Scientific Pretensions by David Berlinski (book, 2008, finished 2016). A mathematician's case that the new atheism claims far more scientific authority than science gives it
- *The Invention of Science*: A New History of the Scientific Revolution by David Wootton (book, 2015, finished 2016). How science was invented between 1572 and 1704, traced through new words such as fact, experiment, and hypothesis
- *Erkenne die Welt*: Eine Geschichte der Philosophie, Band 1 by Richard David Precht (book, 2015, finished December 2015). The first volume of Precht's history of philosophy, from the pre-Socratics to the end of the Middle Ages
- *Cloud Atlas* by David Mitchell (novel, 2004, finished November 2015). Six stories nested inside each other, from a nineteenth-century Pacific voyage to a far future after the fall
- *The Silk Roads*: A New History of the World by Peter Frankopan (book, 2015, finished September 2015). World history told from the trade routes between East and West rather than from Europe
- *Antifragile*: Things That Gain from Disorder by Nassim Nicholas Taleb (book, 2012, finished 2015). Things that gain from disorder, and why systems built to avoid all stress grow fragile
- *Geld aus dem Nichts*: Wie Banken Wachstum ermöglichen und Krisen verursachen by Mathias Binswanger (book, 2015, finished 2015). How commercial banks create money by lending, and what that means for growth and for crises
- *Die Geschichte der Kunst* by E. H. Gombrich (book, 1950, finished January 2014). Gombrich's history of art from the cave paintings to the modern era, the German edition of The Story of Art
- *Die Psychologie von C. G. Jung* by Jolande Jacobi (book, 1940, finished June 2012). An introduction to Jung's analytical psychology by one of his closest collaborators, with a foreword by Jung
- *Demons* by Fyodor Dostoevsky (novel, 1872, finished 2012). A small revolutionary cell in a provincial Russian town and the ideas that lead it to murder
- *The Brothers Karamazov* by Fyodor Dostoevsky (novel, 1880, finished 2011). Three brothers, their father's murder, and a long argument about faith, doubt, and freedom
- *A Little History of the World* by E. H. Gombrich (book, 1936, finished 2011). World history written for children in 1935 by a young art historian, from the Stone Age to the twentieth century
- *Crime and Punishment* by Fyodor Dostoevsky (novel, 1866, finished 2010). A poor former student commits a murder to prove a theory about himself and cannot live with it

## Set aside

- *Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs* by Harold Abelson, Gerald Jay Sussman, and Julie Sussman (book, 1985). The classic MIT course on programming as abstraction, built in Scheme, up to writing interpreters and compilers
